Use existing airfields, ports, bases, factories, warehouses, depots, rail yards, road hubs, power facilities, and civilian distribution centers as logistics nodes. Add a node only when an existing entity cannot represent the facility.

A logistics node has:
- stable entity ID and facility type;
- geographic location;
- owner/operator and access permissions;
- capacity by resource class;
- current stock and reserved stock;
- throughput per simulation interval;
- condition, damage, and repair state;
- staffing and power/service availability;
- security/accessibility state;
- inbound/outbound connections;
- operating schedule and disruption history.

Stock must not be duplicated when cargo is in transit. A transfer reserves or removes stock at origin according to a documented transaction model and creates an in-transit shipment with a single authoritative quantity.

##### Transport network

Represent road, rail, sea, and air transport as graph connections with capacity, travel-time bands, access restrictions, condition, ownership, and disruption state. The system should calculate abstract route feasibility and delivery estimates, not expose real-world interdiction or attack optimization.

Connections may be closed, degraded, congested, reserved, or restored. Weather and disasters may affect them through Chapter 12. Infrastructure damage and repair remain owned by Chapter 12. Logistics reads the authoritative condition rather than duplicating it.

Transport assets can include trucks, trains, cargo ships, cargo aircraft, and civilian contractors. Use existing entity registries and finite capacities. A transport mission or shipment must have a lifecycle and a single owner for its cargo.

##### Shipments and chain of custody

Each shipment record includes:
- shipment ID;
- origin and destination node IDs;
- resource IDs and quantities;
- dispatch, estimated arrival, actual arrival, and cancellation times;
- assigned transport asset or abstract capacity reservation;
- ownership and payer;
- priority and purpose;
- route/connection references;
- loss, damage, delay, diversion, or partial-delivery state;
- loading/unloading events;
- source and destination inventory transaction IDs.

A shipment may be split only through explicit child shipment records whose quantities reconcile to the parent. Partial delivery, spoilage, damage, diversion, and return-to-origin must be represented without double counting.


Connect the existing industry and national finance systems. Facilities have abstract production capacity, input requirements, workforce, energy availability, maintenance condition, and output. Production must consume inputs and create outputs through ledger transactions.

Procurement may be domestic, allied, commercial, leased, donated, captured, or emergency. Every acquisition records source, legal status, price or transfer basis, delivery state, and compatibility. Captured materiel must not automatically become usable: ownership, inspection, maintenance, training, and supply compatibility still apply.

Contracts must reference existing countries, companies, PMCs, and finance records. Do not create a parallel business registry.

##### Demand, prioritization, and shortages

Demand may originate from:
- unit operating consumption;
- maintenance and repair;
- airfield and naval-base operations;
- civilian utilities and public services;
- hospitals and emergency response;
- reconstruction projects;
- training and replacement programs.

Prioritization rules must be explicit, configurable by national policy, and auditable. Shortages should have visible causes: insufficient production, transport capacity, damaged route, inaccessible node, funding, supplier delay, or excessive demand. Do not randomly remove stock.

Support rationing, substitutions where valid, emergency reserves, and negotiated transfers. A shortage in one region must not automatically imply a global shortage if disconnected stock remains elsewhere.

##### Reconciliation with ammunition and expenditure ledgers

The inventory ledger records issue, loading, unloading, firing, expenditure, return, loss, interception, and disposal as distinct transactions. Chapter 14 destruction and expenditure ledger owns campaign-wide fired/expended counts and object-destruction totals. Logistics consumes and reconciles those events; it must not independently increment a second shell counter.

Use idempotent event processing and unique transaction IDs. A replayed event must not consume stock twice. If telemetry is incomplete, flag the discrepancy rather than silently inventing a correction.


Maintenance demand should be generated by the existing aircraft/vehicle/ship serviceability systems. Logistics supplies the required parts and labor capacity. Readiness changes only after the authoritative maintenance workflow records work completion.

Support scheduled maintenance, unscheduled repair, inspection, cannibalization where the game already models it, depot-level work, and return to service. Do not invent technical repair instructions. Show queue, estimated completion, blockers, and resource consumption.

##### Civilian and humanitarian logistics

Civilian supply networks must remain distinct from military stockpiles even where they share transport infrastructure. Food, water, medical supplies, heating/cooling resources, and reconstruction materials should be routed through civilian institutions and humanitarian organizations with their own permissions and accounting.

Military requisition or diversion of civilian goods must be represented as a consequential, legally reviewable event, not as a free transfer. Humanitarian assistance must not automatically become military supply.

##### User interface

Provide:
- national logistics overview;
- node stock and capacity detail;
- shipment tracking;
- production and procurement queues;
- shortage and demand reports;
- transport network status;
- maintenance supply blockers;
- civilian/humanitarian distribution status;
- resource transaction audit.

Use map overlays only when relevant and preserve the existing global map. Do not require the player to micromanage every shipment. Strategic automation may handle routine transfers under explicit policies.


- Inventory is conserved across origin, transit, destination, loss, and return.
- A shipment cannot exist as full stock at both origin and destination.
- Partial deliveries reconcile exactly.
- Replayed shipment or firing events do not duplicate transactions.
- A disconnected depot cannot supply a unit merely because it exists elsewhere on the map.
- Weather and infrastructure disruptions affect shared network availability consistently.
- Production consumes inputs and records outputs.
- Captured equipment is not treated as automatically compatible or serviceable.
- Civilian and humanitarian inventories remain distinct from military inventories.
- Chapter 14 destruction and expenditure ledger ammunition totals reconcile with inventory transactions.
- Save/load, long campaign, and multiplayer tests preserve ledger integrity.



**DEFENSE PROCUREMENT, ACQUISITION, AND SUPPLIER COMPETITION**


Represent procurement as a long, uncertain institutional process rather than instant purchase of equipment.

##### Program lifecycle
Requirements, market research, concept study, competition, prototype, evaluation, contract award, development, testing, production, delivery, acceptance, sustainment, upgrade, cancellation, and retirement.

##### Actors
Governments, service branches, procurement agencies, manufacturers, subcontractors, research institutions, auditors, and export authorities have distinct roles and incentives.

##### Program risks
Track schedule, cost, technical maturity, supplier concentration, workforce, material availability, political support, testing outcomes, and integration dependencies. Programs may be delayed, reduced, re-scoped, or cancelled.

##### Competition and governance
Represent bids, evaluation criteria, conflicts of interest, transparency, industrial policy, domestic capacity, export controls, and oversight. Avoid assuming that lowest price always wins or that a manufacturer's claim proves operational service.

##### Deliveries and fielding
Production and delivery consume finite industrial capacity and logistics. Acceptance tests must pass before inventory becomes operationally available.


Connect the existing weapons catalogue, equipment registry, defense-industry programs, industrial/material systems, finance, workforce, and military maintenance.


No platform or munition enters operational inventory solely because a contract was signed. Delays and cancellations preserve financial and historical records.


**CIVILIANS CAN FOUND, OWN, GROW, AND OPERATE THEIR OWN PMCs**

Add a persistent private military and security company (PMC/PMSC) ecosystem to the campaign. **Civilian characters must be able to independently establish their own companies without the player creating them or giving them an order.** The world should be able to produce new companies as a consequence of insecurity, demand for protection, government outsourcing, available capital, veteran employment, commercial opportunity, and local political conditions. Some companies should remain small and local; a small number may grow into influential multinational organizations. Others should fail, be dissolved, be acquired, lose their licenses, split into rival companies, or become illegal armed organizations.

This is a living-world system, not a static list of pre-generated contractors. The player should occasionally encounter a company that did not exist earlier in the campaign, learn who founded it, see where it operates, and observe how its decisions affect the war and surrounding civilian population.

##### Definition and separation from other organizations

- Treat a PMC/PMSC as a civilian-owned or privately controlled organization that provides contracted security, protection, military-support, or other permitted services. Its legal status and permitted activities depend on the campaign's laws, jurisdiction, contract, and scenario settings.
- Keep PMCs distinct from national armed forces, police, national guard, local defense militias, insurgencies, terrorist organizations, criminal groups, ordinary unarmed contractors, humanitarian organizations, and foreign volunteer formations.
- A PMC is not automatically a terrorist group, militia, proxy force, or government unit. Its ownership, mandate, conduct, legal registration, and actual activities determine how other actors classify it.
- Do not automatically turn every construction, shipping, logistics, technology, or utility company into a PMC because it hires guards. An ordinary business may employ unarmed security or contract a licensed security provider without becoming an armed company.
- A company may establish a separately registered security subsidiary or division when the law and scenario allow it. Keep its commercial parent, armed subsidiary, personnel, assets, financial records, and legal responsibilities linked but distinct.
- Record the difference between a registered company operating within its license, a company operating outside the scope of its contract, an unlicensed armed organization, and a company that has formally lost or surrendered its legal status.
- Do not assume every PMC works for a government or one faction. Companies may serve local authorities, private infrastructure operators, shipping firms, industrial companies, or other clients, subject to legal permissions and the campaign's rules.

##### Civilian founders and autonomous company creation

Generate potential founders from the existing civilian population and personnel systems. Possible founders include entrepreneurs, former military or police personnel, retired security managers, logistics business owners, local business leaders, investors, and groups of people who decide to establish a company together. These are examples, not mandatory templates. Do not make every founder a veteran or assume that all veterans want to work in the security industry.

Each potential founder should be a persistent person or group of people with existing identity, biography, relationships, finances, skills, reputation, motivations, and location. Use the authoritative civilian/personnel records already defined by the campaign. Do not create a second person database for PMC founders.

Allow company formation to emerge from a combination of campaign conditions, including:
- A local or national security gap that existing state and civilian services cannot adequately cover.
- Demand for protection of lawful commercial assets, transport, ports, energy facilities, industrial sites, or other infrastructure.
- Government decisions to outsource specific support or protective services.
- A pool of willing and appropriately qualified people seeking employment after military service, demobilization, displacement, or a change in occupation.
- Available startup capital, investors, premises, equipment, insurance, and access to lawful registration.
- A founder's relationships, organizational ability, reputation, risk tolerance, and willingness to accept the legal and financial responsibilities of the business.
- Local stability, public trust, economic opportunity, licensing policy, and the actual threat environment.

No single condition should automatically create a PMC. A founder may consider the idea and abandon it, fail to secure funding, fail a licensing review, be unable to hire enough personnel, or decide that the risk is too high. Conversely, a company may be created by several founders or an existing civilian business group rather than one individual.

The simulation must create companies while the player is elsewhere or offline within the campaign's supported background-simulation model. Do not require the player to visit a town, open a menu, or complete a mission for civilian founders to act. Creation should be event-driven and rate-limited so that the world does not generate hundreds of companies in response to one repeated condition.

##### Company formation, registration, and growth stages

Model company creation as a sequence of persistent stages rather than instant spawning:
1. **Concept:** one or more civilians consider establishing a company. The proposal records its intended service area, likely clients, founders, and initial business goals.
2. **Organization:** the founders identify ownership, leadership, responsibilities, initial capital, premises, and a proposed operating structure.
3. **Registration and review:** the company applies to the relevant jurisdiction. The review may consider ownership transparency, financial capacity, personnel eligibility, proposed activities, weapons or equipment permissions, insurance, and legal restrictions.
4. **Startup:** the new company obtains premises, administrative staff, initial equipment, insurance or other required guarantees, and its first employees.
5. **Initial operation:** it begins with limited personnel, assets, service coverage, and financial reserves. It must earn or secure contracts before expanding.
6. **Growth or contraction:** the company may hire, train, lease or purchase permitted equipment, open offices, gain clients, lose contracts, or reduce its workforce in response to performance and finances.
7. **Restructuring or exit:** it may merge, be acquired, sell a division, enter insolvency protection, suspend operations, dissolve, or be liquidated. These changes must preserve relevant personnel, equipment, contracts, debts, and historical records.

Each stage takes campaign time and consumes resources. Do not create a fully equipped battalion, fleet, or multinational corporation in one simulation tick. Formation speed and starting scale should reflect founder resources, local law, supply availability, and scenario settings.

##### Corporate identity, ownership, and internal governance

Every company needs a persistent identity and organizational record. Track:
- Stable company ID, legal name, common name, callsign or short designation where relevant, founding date, founding event, headquarters, registered jurisdiction, and operating locations.
- Founders, owners, shareholders or partners, board members where applicable, chief executive, operations director, legal/compliance lead, finance lead, personnel lead, and relevant local managers.
- Ownership shares or control relationships, succession arrangements, internal disputes, conflicts of interest, and changes in control.
- Company logo, visual identity, uniforms, vehicle markings, public image, and historical changes. Cosmetic identity must never substitute for actual legal status or faction affiliation.
- Company size, service specializations, available personnel, deployed personnel, assets, offices, facilities, financial condition, current contracts, and obligations.
- Internal policies covering personnel conduct, protection of civilians, reporting, discipline, use-of-force authorization, complaints, medical care, and cooperation with lawful investigations.
- Management quality, corruption risk, transparency, compliance, labor practices, safety culture, and willingness to cooperate with oversight.

Company leaders must have individual personalities, goals, loyalties, relationships, risk tolerance, public reputations, and personal histories. A founder's death, resignation, arrest, capture, retirement, or loss of confidence may trigger a succession dispute, a board takeover, a company split, a sale, or a controlled transition. It must not automatically delete the company or its staff.

##### Recruitment, employment, and personnel welfare

PMCs recruit people from the existing civilian population and eligible personnel pools. Recruitment must be voluntary and represented as employment, not as an unlimited manpower-generation button.

- Potential employees may include experienced security professionals, veterans, former service members, logistics workers, mechanics, medics, communications staff, pilots and aircrew where qualified and legally permitted, administrators, drivers, interpreters, and other specialists.
- Every recruited person must be an existing canonical person record or a properly generated new person record. A person cannot simultaneously be counted as active national military personnel and as an available PMC employee unless the campaign explicitly records a lawful reserve, leave, secondment, or other compatible status.
- Track applications, offers, acceptance, employment terms, qualifications, contract duration, assigned role, availability, leave, fatigue, injury, medical status, family obligations where modeled, morale, cohesion, and reasons for leaving.
- Recruitment depends on wages, benefits, working conditions, local safety, public reputation, company discipline, employer reliability, legal restrictions, personal preferences, and competing employment opportunities.
- The company must pay wages and account for payroll, insurance, medical care, transport, accommodation, equipment, leave, and other operating costs where applicable. Delayed or unpaid wages can reduce retention, trust, morale, and readiness.
- Do not make all civilians available for recruitment. Essential civilian services, family commitments, age, health, qualifications, legal eligibility, personal beliefs, and individual choices must matter.
- Do not use nationality, ethnicity, religion, or political identity as an automatic indicator of willingness, loyalty, competence, or propensity for violence.
- Companies may lose staff to resignation, competing offers, family relocation, injury, death, capture, legal disqualification, or a decision to return to civilian life. Maintain humane and non-graphic personnel records.
- Personnel who leave a PMC retain their biography and employment history. They may join another company, return to ordinary civilian work, enter a state service if eligible, retire, or relocate.

A company's personnel count must reconcile with the global person registry and existing force-accounting rules. Employees assigned to an operation, attached to a client, hospitalized, on leave, or in transit must never be double-counted.

##### Qualifications, standards, and company capability

Represent company capability through its actual people, qualifications, organization, equipment, readiness, and sustainment—not through one arbitrary combat rating.

- Track role-relevant qualifications and their validity using the existing qualification and certificate systems where applicable.
- Distinguish experienced employees from newly hired staff, personnel in orientation, personnel undergoing qualification, and personnel authorized for a specific role.
- Model company standards, internal evaluations, safety practices, leadership quality, cohesion, communications reliability, medical support, and ability to coordinate with a client.
- Training and professional development take time, qualified instructors, facilities, funding, and available personnel. Represent training outcomes at a high level; do not turn the feature into real-world tactical instruction.
- A company that expands too quickly may have inexperienced managers, insufficient supervisors, uneven standards, and poor integration. A company that loses experienced staff may lose capability even when its headcount remains high.
- Companies may specialize in protective security, site guarding, transport and convoy protection, maritime security, aviation support, maintenance, logistics, medical evacuation support, infrastructure security, or other scenario-approved services.
- Any armed or military-support role must be explicitly bounded by applicable law, contract authority, client permissions, and campaign rules. A company cannot gain a legal mandate merely by purchasing equipment or hiring former soldiers.

##### Equipment ownership, procurement, and sustainment

PMCs may own, lease, borrow, or receive permitted equipment through the existing commercial procurement, arms-trade, logistics, and asset ownership systems. Use the same canonical aircraft, vehicle, ship, weapon, communications, and support-asset records as the rest of the campaign.

- Equipment access depends on local law, export controls, sanctions, supplier willingness, client agreements, available stock, delivery routes, maintenance support, and financial capacity.
- Do not create unlimited weapons or equipment simply because a company wins a contract. Procurement has cost, lead time, delivery, acceptance, storage, maintenance, and training requirements.
- Distinguish company-owned assets, leased assets, client-provided equipment, government-loaned equipment, seized assets, and equipment whose ownership is disputed.
- Record serials, registration, condition, inventory, maintenance, damage, loss, repair, serviceability, and final disposition using existing asset systems.
- Aircraft used by a PMC must use the game's existing flight, crew, maintenance, airspace, and damage systems. Do not introduce a second flight model. Private aviation should be scenario- and law-dependent, and an aircraft's private ownership does not automatically authorize armed operations.
- Company equipment must have fuel, spare parts, ammunition where legally applicable, maintenance staff, storage, and transport constraints. A company that cannot sustain its assets must ground, mothball, lease, sell, or abandon them according to the existing asset rules.
- Equipment transfers between a PMC and a state, faction, client, or another company must update one authoritative ownership record and create a historical transaction event.

##### Contracts, clients, and service obligations

Create a persistent contract system connecting companies to governments, local authorities, commercial operators, infrastructure owners, shipping firms, and other eligible clients. A contract is a legal and financial commitment with a defined scope—not a generic order that makes the PMC loyal to the client forever.

Each contract should contain:
- Contract ID, issuing client, contracted company, legal jurisdiction, signing parties, approval authority, start date, expiry date, renewal conditions, and cancellation clauses.
- Defined service scope, supported locations, authorized responsibilities, required personnel or asset availability, service hours, expected outputs, and any explicit restrictions.
- Budget, payment schedule, currency, funding source, operating costs, insurance or guarantees, penalties, dispute procedures, and outstanding payments.
- Legal authority, license requirements, rules and limitations governing use of force, reporting obligations, civilian-protection requirements, access permissions, and independent oversight.
- Performance measures tied to the actual service requested, plus a record of incidents, delays, failures, complaints, investigations, and verified outcomes.
- Force-protection and personnel-welfare obligations, including medical support, recovery arrangements, and notification procedures where appropriate.

Potential service contracts include protection of specified facilities, security support for ports and transport hubs, convoy and logistics protection, maritime escort or anti-piracy security where permitted by the scenario, evacuation support, personnel recovery assistance, site access control, infrastructure protection, transport, maintenance, medical support, and other bounded support functions.

A scenario may allow a company to provide limited armed security or defensive operational support when legally authorized. Represent its participation through the same campaign mission, unit, rules-of-engagement, and outcome systems used by all other forces. Do not supply real-world tactical procedures or allow a contract to authorize attacks on civilians. Offensive combat work, weapons use, detention authority, cross-border activity, and intelligence activity must never be assumed to be lawful merely because a client requests them.

Companies may submit bids, negotiate terms, reject a contract, request changes, or withdraw when legally and contractually permitted. Clients may compare price, availability, reputation, capability, compliance history, insurance, political exposure, and previous performance. A contract must not be awarded solely because the company is nearby or has the largest unit count.

Contracts can be delayed, disputed, amended, suspended, breached, terminated, or completed. A government may cancel a contract after a ceasefire or leadership change; a private client may stop paying; a PMC may refuse an unlawful or out-of-scope order. Such events create financial, legal, political, and personnel consequences rather than instantly deleting the associated company or unit.

##### Company autonomy, loyalty, and behavior during the war

PMCs are independent organizations with obligations, incentives, constraints, and leadership decisions. They are not automatically subordinate to the faction that happens to hire them.

- Give every company a relationship profile with clients, governments, factions, local communities, suppliers, regulators, employees, and competing companies.
- Separate legal domicile, ownership nationality, operating location, current client, political sympathies, and actual allegiance. These are different properties and may conflict.
- A company may be based in a neutral country, owned by citizens of one country, operate in another region, and contract with a third party, subject to applicable permissions.
- Do not let a company freely contract with opposing belligerents for incompatible services at the same time. Apply conflict-of-interest checks, disclosure rules, contract separation, and political consequences.
- A company can remain neutral, serve one side, change clients after a contract ends, or become politically aligned over time. A change in alignment must be driven by leadership decisions, ownership, law, threats, finances, and contract history—not by a random faction flip.
- Companies may decline contracts because of risk, insufficient capability, poor payment history, legal exposure, employee opposition, sanctions, or internal policy.
- Companies may prioritize profitable clients over less profitable communities, but this can damage public trust and create political backlash. Some may accept lower returns to preserve local legitimacy or honor an existing commitment.
- Companies may compete for contracts, personnel, suppliers, facilities, and reputation. Competition can be commercial, political, or legal; do not make every company a hostile armed rival.
- Model rare serious failures—contract fraud, corruption, mistreatment, unlawful actions, internal factional disputes, desertion, or rogue leadership—as incidents with evidence, investigation, uncertainty, and consequences. Do not assume guilt from rumor alone.
- A company that becomes criminal or operates outside the law may lose its PMC registration and transition into a different non-state actor category through a recorded legal and organizational event. Do not silently relabel every poorly performing company as a criminal group.

##### Financial survival and the possibility of failure

A PMC must have an actual economic lifecycle. Track available cash, accounts receivable, debt, payroll, operating costs, insurance, taxes or fees where represented, equipment leases, maintenance obligations, contract revenue, investment, and financial reserves.

- Startup capital may come from the founders, disclosed investors, commercial loans, or lawful financing sources represented at an abstract level.
- Contracts create revenue only when the company meets the agreed payment conditions. A signed contract does not instantly grant unlimited spendable money.
- The company must pay for personnel, equipment, facilities, transport, communications, medical support, maintenance, and other relevant services.
- Poor performance, non-payment, loss of assets, sanctions, legal disputes, excessive expansion, reputational damage, or a decline in demand can create insolvency.
- A profitable company may expand, build reserves, invest in training, maintain better equipment, or open new offices. Growth must still be limited by hiring, procurement, legal review, and sustainment capacity.
- A company may downsize, sell assets, restructure debt, merge, be acquired, enter insolvency proceedings, or close. Preserve employee outcomes and asset disposition.
- Do not let bankruptcy erase unpaid wages, casualties, crimes, contract disputes, damaged assets, debts, or the historical record.
- Insurers, lenders, investors, and suppliers may change their terms based on the company's actual risk and reliability. Do not model these as omniscient; they act on available information.

##### Legal status, oversight, and accountability

Legal status must be jurisdiction-specific and configurable. Different countries and campaign settings may use different licensing, registration, procurement, and oversight systems. Do not apply one universal real-world legal interpretation to every fictional country.

Track registration, operating licenses, permitted services, weapons permissions where relevant, export restrictions, sanctions, contract authority, jurisdiction, insurance, reporting, investigations, and suspension or revocation decisions.

- A license is not a guarantee of good conduct, and a good reputation is not a substitute for legal authorization.
- Governments may approve, limit, audit, suspend, or revoke a company's license. The process takes time and may be contested or politically influenced.
- Independent courts, inspectors, commissions, client auditors, and investigative bodies may review allegations and verified incidents according to their jurisdiction and access.
- Maintain evidence provenance and distinguish allegation, suspicion, investigation, charge, adjudication, and established finding.
- A company may cooperate with investigators, dispute jurisdiction, provide records, conceal information, or challenge an action through represented legal processes. These choices affect trust and consequences.
- Personnel must have access to appropriate medical support and a process to report unsafe or unlawful conduct. Complaints and whistleblower events should be tracked without automatically assuming they are true or false.
- Civilian protection rules in Chapter 09 apply to PMCs exactly as they apply to state forces and other armed actors. A private contract cannot authorize deliberate attacks on civilian populations, punishment of civilians, or optimization of fear and civilian harm.
- If a PMC causes or is credibly suspected of causing civilian harm, preserve the event record, support civilian response, and route evidence through the existing investigation and accountability systems. Keep civilian casualties separate from military and PMC personnel losses.

##### Civilian community effects and public reputation

The presence of a PMC changes the community around it. Model local reactions as varied and evidence-driven rather than uniformly supportive or hostile.

- A company may create jobs, pay wages, purchase local services, protect a facility, support evacuation, or help keep transport operating.
- Its presence may also increase tension, create noise and traffic, compete for housing or labor, raise insurance costs, or make a town appear more militarized.
- Residents may support a company because it provides security, oppose it because they distrust private armed organizations, remain indifferent, or hold mixed views depending on personal experience.
- Track public reputation separately from government approval, client satisfaction, employee morale, and legal standing. These values should not collapse into one score.
- Local officials may negotiate operating conditions, restrict access, demand transparency, or refuse a company's presence. Community complaints may cause review or contract changes.
- The company may support local disaster response or humanitarian logistics when appropriately authorized and when doing so does not misrepresent it as a neutral humanitarian organization.
- Do not reward a PMC for generating insecurity that it then profits from. Any involvement in creating or prolonging a threat must be treated as a serious allegation with evidence and major legal, political, and reputational consequences.

##### Competition, mergers, internal factions, and organizational change

As the campaign evolves, companies should be able to change scale and structure.

- Allow mergers, acquisitions, spin-offs, subsidiaries, changes of ownership, executive succession, management buyouts, and dissolutions.
- Allow internal disagreements over risk, profit, legality, political alignment, employee treatment, and contract choices.
- A division may leave and form a new company only through a recorded founding process with real personnel, assets, capital, and legal status. Do not duplicate its people or equipment in the process.
- Competing companies may bid against each other, share subcontractors, form temporary joint ventures, or dispute contract awards.
- A parent company may own multiple service divisions, but each division's mandate, staff, assets, and liabilities must be clear.
- If a company loses its founder or a major client, its future should depend on succession, finances, leadership quality, staff confidence, and outstanding obligations.
- Company names, logos, histories, and reputation records persist after a merger or closure so campaign history remains understandable.

##### Player interaction and campaign interface

Create an interface that makes the PMC ecosystem understandable without forcing the player to become a corporate manager.

Provide a **Private Security / PMC Registry** or an equivalent entry in the existing campaign organization interface. It should display only information the player's faction or character is entitled to know. For each known company, show:
- Company name, identity, founder or leadership when known, home jurisdiction, known operating areas, and date founded.
- Legal status and license state, with uncertainty or disputed status clearly indicated.
- Known services, approximate size, available or deployed strength where intelligence supports it, known assets, and current or recent contracts.
- Client relationships, reputation, notable public events, verified investigations, and financial health only where the information is public or legitimately obtained.
- Company history, growth, mergers, contract changes, and major incidents.

The player may encounter PMC personnel and assets during missions, see their markings, hear about contracts and disputes through news or briefings, escort or cooperate with them under an authorized mission, protect civilians from an unlawful actor, or report suspected misconduct. These interactions must use existing mission and event systems.

Do not make every PMC globally visible on the map. The player may know a registered headquarters exists but not know a company's deployed personnel, equipment, or current contract details without reporting or intelligence. Rumors must remain rumors until corroborated.

Optional investment, sponsorship, management, or player-founded-company mechanics may be added only if the existing campaign has a compatible civilian or management role. They are not required for the core feature. **NPC civilians founding and operating PMCs autonomously is mandatory and must not be gated behind player interaction.** The player's normal pilot career and flight gameplay must remain fully functional without managing any PMC.

##### Campaign events, news, and narrative history

Publish meaningful PMC events to the existing campaign event ledger and news system. Examples include:
- A civilian founder announces a new company or applies for registration.
- A regulator approves, restricts, suspends, or revokes a license.
- A company hires a known veteran, opens a regional office, or receives its first contract.
- A contract is awarded, renewed, disputed, completed, or terminated.
- A company convoy or facility is protected, delayed, damaged, or evacuated.
- A company wins or loses a major client, acquires equipment, or expands to another region.
- A payment dispute causes layoffs, a strike, or a withdrawal from service.
- An investigation finds evidence of misconduct, clears an allegation, or leaves a case unresolved.
- A company merges, changes ownership, splits, becomes insolvent, or closes.

News reports must distinguish verified facts, company statements, client statements, allegations, rumors, and intelligence assessments. Preserve the underlying event even if a company later changes its name or ownership. People should remember companies that helped them, failed them, or harmed their community.

##### Autonomous AI decisions and simulation scale

Company AI must use the same campaign time, resource limits, knowledge boundaries, and event authority as other civilian organizations.

- Run a low-cost strategic decision model for companies far from players and instantiate detailed personnel and assets only when relevant.
- Use existing chunk streaming and background simulation. A PMC must retain headquarters, staff, contracts, finances, asset locations, and history while its map region is unloaded.
- Founding, hiring, procurement, contract bidding, movement, and dissolution must be represented as scheduled or event-driven decisions, not high-frequency per-frame logic.
- Companies must act on known information. A leader cannot know hidden enemy deployments, private government plans, or events outside its reporting network unless the company obtains that information through a recorded source.
- A company's decisions should be constrained by staff, cash, equipment, maintenance, fuel, legal status, transport, contract scope, and willingness of employees.
- Avoid global pathfinding and tactical AI for every PMC asset every frame. Use strategic task and route summaries for distant units and detailed behavior only near active simulation areas.
- Company size and spawn frequency must have configurable limits. The campaign should feel populated but not generate an endless number of insignificant entities.

##### Canonical data model and persistence requirements

Integrate PMCs with the existing organization, personnel, unit, asset, event, finance, contract, and legal-record systems. Do not create parallel copies of information already stored elsewhere.

A PMC organization record should reference, rather than duplicate:
- Existing person IDs for founders, owners, managers, employees, and former employees.
- Existing unit IDs for security teams, support teams, detachments, and other formations.
- Existing asset IDs for aircraft, vehicles, vessels, weapons, facilities, and equipment.
- Existing contract IDs, finance ledger transactions, procurement records, licenses, investigations, and campaign events.
- Existing regional IDs, base/facility IDs, supply nodes, and map ownership references.

The organization record should own company-specific identity, control, corporate relationships, legal registration, service specializations, reputation dimensions, internal policies, and references to active obligations. Use stable IDs and explicit state transitions. Store founding event, ownership history, leadership succession, legal changes, company mergers, and closure as durable historical events.

Update campaign JSON export/import, browser persistence, migration, multiplayer host authority, and save validation. Validate references, ownership, personnel uniqueness, asset uniqueness, contract consistency, legal status, nonnegative inventory, finance reconciliation, and valid state transitions. A company may not be loaded with more employees, vehicles, or aircraft than the authoritative records contain.

##### Multiplayer and authority

In cooperative campaigns, the authoritative campaign host owns PMC creation, finances, recruitment, contracts, asset transfers, personnel status, legal outcomes, and company AI decisions. Clients receive replicated results and permitted information.

- Prevent a client from fabricating a PMC, creating employees, granting equipment, changing ownership, awarding a contract, or editing a company's financial ledger.
- Apply the campaign's existing permissions to player interactions with a PMC. A player cannot issue orders to a company merely because it is friendly or has a contract with the same faction.
- Keep secret contracts, personnel details, protected client information, and intelligence assessments behind existing access controls.
- Ensure all players see the same committed company identity, asset ownership, contract state, and public event history.
- Reconnection must restore the current authoritative state without replaying company founding, recruitment, payments, or asset-transfer events as new events.

---

#### Operational behavior, AI support, and coordination
**Global air operations, theater planning, and dynamic air mission generation**

- Generate missions from actual campaign needs, not random mission templates alone.
- Support offensive counter-air, defensive counter-air, combat air patrol, fighter sweep, interception, bomber interception, escort, strike escort, and high-value asset defense.
- Support SEAD, DEAD, radar reconnaissance, emitter location, electronic attack support, decoy support, and air-defense network assessment.
- Support close air support, battlefield air interdiction, armed reconnaissance, convoy escort, artillery spotting, and emergency ground-force support.
- Support deep strike, infrastructure attack, runway denial, logistics interdiction, maritime strike, anti-submarine patrol, and fleet defense.
- Support reconnaissance, photo intelligence, electronic intelligence, signals intelligence, weather reconnaissance, damage assessment, and persistent surveillance.
- Support combat search and rescue, personnel recovery, pilot escort, medical evacuation, humanitarian aid, civilian evacuation, and emergency supply delivery.
- Support special operations insertion and extraction, surveillance support, communication relay, and recovery of isolated teams.
- Support defensive counteroffensives, reinforcement cover, withdrawal cover, evacuation cover, and protection of retreating units.
- Support alert scrambles, quick reaction alert, airborne patrols, barrier CAP, night defense, and long-duration combat air patrols.
- Support carrier operations, deck cycles, launch queues, recovery windows, marshal stacks, bolters, and divert decisions.
- Every mission should include a reason it exists, a strategic context, available intelligence, friendly assets, enemy capability estimates, expected risks, and a clear success impact.
- Missions should have primary, secondary, and optional objectives. Completing an objective should affect the campaign in a specific, visible way.
- Add mission branches and contingencies. The target may move, the weather may worsen, an escort may be delayed, an airfield may be attacked, or a friendly unit may request urgent support.
- Add dynamic retasking by AWACS, ground command, JTAC, carrier command, or theater headquarters.
- Add time-on-target coordination, multi-flight packages, deconfliction, alternate routes, tanker plans, emergency divert plans, and abort criteria.
- Add mission cancellation when the target no longer matters, the intelligence is invalidated, the political situation changes, or the package cannot safely proceed.
- Do not make all missions require destroying something. Some should reward identifying, observing, escorting, protecting, rescuing, delivering, delaying, or successfully avoiding escalation.
- Let mission complexity and threat scale with the actual campaign. An enemy that has lost its radar network should not still generate the same fully coordinated air-defense package.
- Add mission performance evaluation based on mission purpose, protected assets, identification, timing, survival, collateral damage, intelligence value, and strategic effect—not only kill count.

**Global air war and theater campaign behavior.**

- Model air power as a campaign system, not merely a collection of individual dogfights. Aircraft availability, mission generation, basing, support, intelligence, weather, weapons stockpiles, and command priorities must determine what sorties can be flown.
- Add strategic air objectives such as air superiority, airspace denial, protection of friendly forces, defense of population centers, escort of high-value aircraft, maritime surveillance, transport protection, and support to ground or naval operations.
- Add operational air objectives such as suppressing threats, disrupting military movement, protecting reinforcement routes, isolating a battlefield, defending airbases, and supporting withdrawal or counteroffensive operations.
- Add defensive counter-air, offensive counter-air, combat air patrol, interception, escort, point defense, area defense, reconnaissance, tactical strike, close air support, battlefield interdiction, maritime patrol, search and rescue, tanker support, airborne command support, and transport missions.
- Add air campaign planning in daily or configurable cycles. The AI should prioritize missions based on objectives, intelligence confidence, force availability, weather, political restrictions, threat, and expected cost.
- Add sortie generation limits. Aircraft need qualified crews, serviceable engines, inspections, weapons, fuel, maintenance time, and suitable runway conditions.
- Add aircraft dispersal, relocation, alternate airfields, emergency divert bases, highway or austere strips where supported by the scenario, and runway repair.
- Add base vulnerability and resilience. Airbases may be damaged, temporarily closed, partially operational, repaired, dispersed, or supplied by alternate routes.
- Add aircraft losses that affect national airpower over time. Experienced crews, specialized aircraft, tankers, airborne early warning aircraft, electronic-support aircraft, transports, and rescue helicopters should have meaningful scarcity.
- Add aircrew survival, rescue, capture, repatriation, medical recovery, and return-to-duty decisions.
- Add support-aircraft scheduling. Tankers, airborne early warning, electronic warfare, maritime patrol, transports, and search-and-rescue aircraft have finite availability and must be assigned to competing needs.
- Add weather and airfield condition impacts on sortie schedules, takeoff weights, mission cancellation, diversion, and maintenance.
- Add airspace congestion from multiple coalition packages, civilian aircraft, drones, helicopters, transports, and returning flights.
- Add high-value asset protection and relocation. Command aircraft, tankers, radar aircraft, and transport hubs should not remain in predictable, invulnerable locations.
- Add air campaign assessments. Show whether a theater is gaining, losing, or contesting air superiority, while making the estimate dependent on intelligence quality and time period.
- Keep strategic airpower effects plausible and indirect. A campaign-level strike should alter capacity, access, readiness, or infrastructure over time rather than magically erase an entire enemy force.



##### Operational planning interface

Add a player-facing operations room or planning interface that sits above individual mission selection. It should show the theater situation, available squadrons, support assets, intelligence confidence, airbase readiness, weather, fuel and ammunition availability, mission requests, and current operational commitments.

The room is a command and planning interface, not a replacement for the existing flight UI or aircraft systems. The player can plan, approve, modify, delegate, or decline operations and then fly a selected sortie.

##### Package construction

Allow the player to create packages from available assets. Depending on the game content, package roles may include primary mission aircraft, escort, reconnaissance, airborne command and control, refueling, transport, search and rescue, electronic support, and reserve elements.

Every role must be backed by an actual available unit, with real readiness, crew, fuel, maintenance, basing, and scheduling constraints. Do not create a support aircraft simply because the planner needs one.

##### Support and coordination requests

The player can request support from other commands. Requests have a requesting authority, priority, time window, location, purpose, and status. A support command can accept, decline, delay, or offer an alternative based on its own resources and national restrictions.

Examples include tanker support, airborne surveillance, rescue standby, transport, medical evacuation, engineering, maritime patrol, and ground-force coordination. The specific request list should be data-driven.

##### Scheduling and deconfliction

The planner should identify conflicts involving aircraft availability, runway or parking capacity, crew shifts, weather, airspace restrictions, support windows, tanker availability, maintenance, and other operations. Show warnings and feasible alternatives. The planner must not silently resolve a conflict by teleporting or duplicating assets.

##### Mission routes and campaign constraints

Allow routes and mission areas to be planned using the game's existing navigation and map systems. Show relevant uncertainty, known restrictions, alternate bases, recovery options, and support availability. Do not expose information the player has not obtained through campaign intelligence.

##### AI-generated plans and recommendations

AI headquarters can propose plans with objectives, assigned forces, expected resource needs, risks, assumptions, and confidence. The player may approve, modify, delegate, or reject them. AI recommendations should explain their reasoning in concise operational language and disclose major uncertainties.

##### Execution monitoring

Once approved, a plan becomes a persistent operation. Show assets assigned, launched, delayed, aborted, lost, diverted, recovered, or reassigned. A plan can change because of weather, new intelligence, aircraft faults, political decisions, support losses, or changing campaign priorities.

##### Debrief and lessons learned

After an operation, record planned versus actual execution, resource expenditure, mission outcomes, asset condition, intelligence changes, notable events, and recommendations. Feed relevant data into squadron history and AI learning without treating a single outcome as proof that a tactic is universally effective.

##### Planning room acceptance tests

Verify that unavailable aircraft cannot be assigned, support requests can be rejected, schedule conflicts are visible, weather updates affect plans, a damaged base restricts capacity, and an approved plan persists after save/load. Verify that a planning interface cannot bypass existing aircraft readiness or flight systems.

**Unit organization, behavior, and simulation requirements**

- Organize units into realistic but configurable echelons: team or section, platoon, company, battalion, regiment or brigade, division, corps, army, fleet, air force component, and theater command. Not every country needs to use the same structure.
- Allow a unit to be an individual platform, a flight, a battery, a company, a battalion, a ship, a squadron, or an abstract formation depending on simulation scale. Avoid simulating every individual soldier when an aggregate formation produces the same strategic result.
- Give each unit a unique identity, country, service branch, parent formation, commander, home base, current location, mission, readiness, morale, cohesion, experience, equipment state, and supply status.
- Track personnel strength and equipment strength separately. A formation may have all its vehicles but insufficient trained crews, or enough personnel but too few operational vehicles.
- Track fuel, ammunition, spare parts, maintenance capacity, medical support, food, water, communications, and transport access according to the unit's role.
- Track movement type and terrain compatibility: road, off-road, tracked, wheeled, rail, airlift, sealift, amphibious, helicopter lift, or strategic transport.
- Track operational availability: active, reserve, mobilizing, training, deployed, refitting, damaged, recovering, interned, surrendered, disbanded, or destroyed.
- Track sensor capabilities and information quality. A unit's visible map symbol must not imply that the player knows its exact strength, equipment, or mission.
- Give units doctrine and behavior profiles, but let commanders, morale, losses, logistics, weather, terrain, and orders influence what they actually do.
- Let formations split, merge, reinforce, reorganize, re-equip, withdraw, surrender, or be disbanded when campaign conditions justify it.
- Distinguish destroyed equipment, damaged equipment, abandoned equipment, captured equipment, and equipment awaiting repair.
- Allow older equipment to remain in service, especially in reserve formations, smaller countries, and prolonged wars. Older does not automatically mean useless; reliability, training, maintenance, and mission context matter.
- Provide country-specific names, symbols, visual appearance, radio callsigns, organization, and equipment without making all forces cosmetic reskins of the same unit.
- Ensure that the unit roster affects mission generation, logistics, strategic AI, intelligence, fog of war, campaign history, and postwar settlement.

**DYNAMIC GROUND-FORCE BEHAVIOR**

Ground forces must maneuver as living formations, not simply follow a straight line toward a waypoint.


**Combat posture and survival behavior**

- Choose between advancing, holding, defending, taking cover, dispersing, concealing, withdrawing, recovering, and surrendering based on the situation.
- React to incoming threats by changing posture, seeking available protection, reporting the threat, and requesting support.
- Use smoke, concealment, camouflage, defensive positions, obstacles, and decoys as broad game mechanics with limited inventories and imperfect effects.
- Give formations a suppression, cohesion, fatigue, morale, and readiness model. These values should influence movement and command response without replacing the underlying damage model.
- Units can become pinned, disorganized, separated, isolated, low on ammunition, low on fuel, or unable to move due to mechanical failure.
- A unit that is losing a battle should not always fight to destruction. It may withdraw, call for help, leave equipment behind, surrender, or attempt to reconnect with friendly forces.
- A retreat can be orderly, hurried, disorganized, or routed depending on command, cohesion, morale, leadership, terrain, and communications.
- AI should not automatically pursue every retreating enemy. It must consider mission priority, threat, readiness, logistics, potential ambushes, and orders.


**Tactical coordination and support requests**

- Ground formations can request reconnaissance, engineering support, recovery vehicles, resupply, medical evacuation, artillery support, air defense coverage, transport, reinforcements, or permission to withdraw.
- Requests should travel through command networks and may be delayed, denied, partially fulfilled, or answered by an alternate unit.
- Nearby units can support one another, reinforce a threatened position, cover a withdrawal, secure a route, escort a convoy, or establish a temporary reserve.
- Allow AI to identify when it lacks the strength or supplies to continue and to recommend a pause, consolidation, or change of mission.
- Allow coalition units to coordinate across national command boundaries, but include liaison delays, incompatible communications, national restrictions, and disputes over who controls the operation.


**DYNAMIC NAVAL AI**

- Ships should navigate around weather, sea state, traffic, coastal restrictions, mine danger zones as abstract map conditions, fuel, replenishment, damaged ports, and mission boundaries.
- Create and maintain carrier groups, amphibious groups, escort formations, patrol groups, logistics convoys, and submarine patrol assignments.
- Ships can escort, screen, patrol, shadow, investigate, reposition, withdraw, return to port, replenish, conduct search and rescue, or provide humanitarian assistance.
- Surface ships can request air cover, replenishment, repair, medical evacuation, or escort reinforcement.
- Submarines must have uncertain contact information, endurance, maintenance, communications restrictions, and assigned patrol areas. They should not have a perfect real-time map of all ships.
- Naval units should change posture as threat, mission, rules of engagement, and national authorization change.
- Damaged ships can reduce speed, lose sensors, lose propulsion, request towing, seek a friendly port, abandon ship, or become a rescue mission.
- Naval aviation can request deck recovery, tanker support, diversion, or emergency assistance.
- Naval commanders should consider the protection of merchant shipping, sea lanes, ports, and neutral vessels, not just enemy warships.
- Include convoy escorts, replenishment ships, hospital ships, icebreakers, survey vessels, rescue craft, and maritime patrol aircraft as meaningful campaign units.


**CRITICAL SCOPE CORRECTION: DO NOT REBUILD THE EXISTING AIRCRAFT**

The game already has its main aircraft/fighter roster. This request is **not** asking for another set of fighters, interceptors, strike aircraft, or bombers. Preserve all aircraft that already exist, along with their existing flight models, cockpits, weapons, radar, sensors, damage systems, and player controls.

The missing content is the wider military ecosystem that makes a modern war function:

- Uncrewed aircraft and drones of many sizes and roles.
- AWACS and airborne early-warning aircraft.
- Airborne command-post, surveillance, electronic-support, and maritime-patrol platforms.
- Cargo, strategic airlift, tactical transport, aerial refueling, and medical-evacuation support aircraft.
- Surface-to-air missile systems (SAMs), short-range air defense, gun systems, counter-rocket systems, and counter-UAS defenses.
- Air-defense radars, command vehicles, communications relays, launchers, reload vehicles, and support trucks.
- Ground logistics, engineering, recovery, medical, reconnaissance, and command units.
- Naval support, replenishment, patrol, unmanned maritime, and undersea units.
- Uncrewed ground vehicles, deployable sensors, and other supporting systems.

**Do not duplicate existing combat aircraft.** A support aircraft such as an E-3, E-2, E-7, C-17, C-130, A400M, Il-76, Y-20, KC-46, KC-135, A330 MRTT, or YY-20 is a new requested platform class because it performs a support role not covered by the existing fighter roster. Add it only if it is not already present in the project.

Before coding, inspect the current asset database and produce a simple inventory report with three columns: `Already implemented`, `Missing and requested here`, and `Not appropriate for this scenario`. Reuse existing assets wherever possible. Do not overwrite an existing aircraft or vehicle just because this addendum names a variant.

**GROUND SUPPORT UNITS, MOBILE AIR DEFENSE, AND CAMPAIGN SERVICE VEHICLES**

Rework the existing ground-unit model into a consistent force registry that includes combat units and the support units that keep them operating. Do not make every vehicle an isolated icon with no logistics, crew, command, or repair behavior.

##### Air-defense formations

Expand existing SAM sites into coherent air-defense entities where the data model supports them. A site or formation may include command elements, search radar, engagement radar, launcher vehicles, reload vehicles, power support, communications, crew, transport, and maintenance. A fixed installation and a mobile formation must have different deployment and availability behavior.

Track unit status, radar availability, launcher availability, ammunition inventory, reload state, crew readiness, movement, setup or teardown state, power, communications, damage, repair, and command relationship. Keep exact tactical rules at the level appropriate for game simulation; avoid magic omniscient detection or unlimited ammunition.

Include short-, medium-, and long-range air-defense categories, gun-based air defense, mobile point defense, and command / radar support variants. Country equipment lists should remain scenario-configurable and should not assume that all systems are present in every conflict.

##### Ground support and service vehicle registry

Add or expand data-driven roles for:
- Mobile radar and early-warning vehicles.
- Mobile command posts and communications vehicles.
- Electronic-support and communications-relay vehicles.
- Fuel tankers and water tankers.
- Ammunition and general cargo carriers.
- Recovery and heavy repair vehicles.
- Engineer and construction vehicles.
- Bridge-layer and bridging support vehicles.
- Route-clearance and explosive-ordnance-disposal vehicles.
- Ambulances and protected medical evacuation vehicles.
- Field workshop and maintenance vehicles.
- Mobile power generation and utility vehicles.
- Reconnaissance and observation vehicles.
- Airfield repair and runway service vehicles.
- Military police and traffic-control vehicles.

##### Ground unit lifecycle and state

All units should have stable identity, affiliation, location, parent formation, personnel, equipment, readiness, orders, supplies, communications, morale, cohesion, damage, maintenance, and history. Use the detailed personnel and equipment ledgers already specified in Chapters 02, 04, 06, 07, 17, 19 and 20; do not create a second casualty or equipment-count system.

##### Logistics and service behavior

Support vehicles must carry actual inventory or service capacity. Cargo is removed from the source and added to the destination only after a valid transfer. Repair vehicles require parts, technicians, capacity, access, and time. Medical vehicles require capacity and medical supplies. Engineering vehicles require materials and work time. A unit must be able to request support and receive a realistic status such as accepted, queued, dispatched, delayed, unavailable, blocked, or completed.

##### AI unit autonomy

Units should continue following their last valid order when communications are lost, subject to their doctrine and local situation. They may report shortages, damage, movement, casualties, support requests, or mission completion when communications return. They must not know the exact state of unseen enemy units.


- A mobile air-defense unit must consume ammunition and require reloads.
- A radar vehicle and launcher vehicle can have different damage and availability states.
- A damaged support vehicle can reduce the supported formation's capability.
- A supply vehicle cannot deliver more than its recorded cargo capacity.
- A repair vehicle cannot repair without required parts and service capacity.
- Medical evacuation capacity is finite and personnel are not counted as both available and hospitalized.
- A unit with lost communications continues with its last valid order and does not receive hidden new orders.

**COMBAT CLAIM VERIFICATION, EVIDENCE REVIEW, AND DEBRIEF CONFIDENCE**

Expand mission debriefing so a reported kill, damage event, or mission result is not automatically treated as confirmed fact. The campaign should distinguish what happened, what a pilot reported, what sensors observed, and what intelligence later verified.

##### Separate event, claim, and assessment

Maintain separate records for:
- The underlying simulation event, if the authoritative simulation knows what happened.
- The claim made by a pilot, wingman, controller, sensor operator, or mission system.
- The evidence available to the player or command staff at the time.
- The official assessment after review.
- Any later correction or reclassification.

Do not allow a claim to overwrite the underlying event record. Do not expose hidden simulation truth to a player when the player's side has not established it.

##### Assessment categories

Use configurable, clearly explained categories such as:
- Confirmed destroyed.
- Probable destroyed.
- Damaged / mission-killed.
- Probable damage.
- Target departed / disengaged.
- Target lost from sensors; outcome unknown.
- No verified effect.
- Friendly loss / friendly damage.
- Duplicate or invalid claim.
- Disputed assessment.

These categories must be data-driven and should not imply more certainty than the evidence supports.

##### Evidence sources

Allow debrief analysts to consider evidence that was actually collected:
- Flight recorder and weapons-release telemetry.
- Radar and datalink track history.
- AWACS / GCI reports.
- Wingman and other pilot reports.
- RWR and sensor recordings.
- Gun-camera or onboard recording references where supported.
- Reconnaissance imagery and later observations.
- Search-and-rescue reports.
- Debris, wreckage, or site inspection records where the campaign has such data.
- Enemy or neutral public reporting, clearly labeled by source reliability.
- Later intelligence assessments and independent confirmation.

No single evidence type should always be treated as conclusive. For example, a target disappearing from radar does not prove destruction.

##### Scoring and career records

- Distinguish claimed kills from officially credited kills.
- Allow probable or disputed claims to remain pending until further evidence appears.
- Update career records if a claim is later confirmed, downgraded, or disproved.
- Preserve the history of corrections instead of silently rewriting the pilot's record.
- Prevent repeated debriefing or replay from awarding duplicate credit.
- Use consistent attribution rules for shared kills, assists, multi-ship engagements, and uncertain weapons effects.

##### Campaign and media consequences

Verified results may influence public reporting, squadron reputation, political claims, and enemy assessments. Unverified reports may be repeated as claims but must remain labeled as such. News organizations may later issue corrections. Avoid presenting propaganda as ground truth.


- A radar track disappearing creates an uncertain assessment, not an automatic confirmed kill.
- Independent evidence can raise or lower confidence.
- A later correction updates the official record without erasing the original claim.
- Career statistics reconcile with the authoritative claim ledger.
- A player cannot earn duplicate credit by replaying or re-importing a debrief.

**PERSISTENT AIRCRAFT WEATHERING, SERVICE WEAR, AND REPAINT HISTORY**

existing already gives aircraft unique identities, paint, markings, damage history, flight hours, and maintenance records. Add a visual condition system that derives appearance from those existing records.

##### Appearance state

Represent appropriate aircraft-specific visual changes such as:
- General dirt, dust, mud, salt residue, and grime.
- Exhaust staining and fluid marks.
- Paint fading and sun exposure.
- Surface wear around frequently serviced areas.
- Scuffs, abrasions, panel replacement, and repair patches.
- Battle damage and temporary field repairs.
- Repainted markings, replacement panels, and changed squadron insignia when authorized.

Do not apply every effect to every aircraft. Use aircraft type, environment, service history, material, operating location, and maintenance actions to determine suitable appearance changes.

##### Appearance must follow history

- Derive wear from flight hours, operating environment, weather exposure, ground activity, maintenance, damage, and time in service.
- A wash or cleaning task may reduce dirt but must not erase physical damage.
- A repaint or panel replacement requires a real maintenance job, materials, staff, and downtime.
- Battle damage should remain visible until repaired. A cosmetic texture update must not silently repair the underlying aircraft damage state.
- Preserve paint schemes and unit markings through transfers and deployments unless an actual repaint or re-marking event occurs.
- Store a compact appearance state and relevant history, not a full texture copy for every aircraft.

##### Visual implementation

- Use material parameters, decals, texture variants, or other existing rendering techniques.
- Prefer shared materials and instancing-compatible variation over unique heavy textures for every aircraft.
- Apply high-detail wear only to nearby aircraft. Distant aircraft can use simple material variation.
- Provide an option to reduce cosmetic effects for performance.


- An aircraft accumulates appropriate wear over campaign time and service use.
- Washing reduces dirt but does not heal structural damage.
- Repainting requires maintenance time and resources and persists across save/load.
- Aircraft of the same type can have distinct appearance histories without duplicating their base model assets.

---


**FORMAL PILOT, AIRCREW, AND AIRCRAFT CERTIFICATE PRESENTATION**

existing already has training courses, qualifications, endorsements, pilot records, and aircraft condition records. Add a formal certificate and clearance presentation layer that reads and writes those existing records.

##### Pilot and aircrew certificates

Where applicable to the game's systems, present records for:
- Aircraft type qualification.
- Carrier qualification and current landing currency.
- Night or low-visibility qualification where supported.
- Formation and cooperative-flight qualification.
- Refueling qualification.
- Instructor or evaluator status.
- Mission-specific qualification or authorization.
- Multi-crew station qualification.

Each certificate should show issuing authority, holder, aircraft/type scope, date earned, expiry or review date where applicable, status, evidence/training records, and restrictions.

##### Aircraft and maintenance release documents

Provide aircraft-specific service documents such as:
- Preflight inspection status.
- Post-flight inspection status.
- Scheduled inspection status.
- Maintenance release or return-to-service status.
- Deferred defect list where modeled.
- Configuration/loadout verification.
- Component replacement and calibration records.

A certificate or release is valid only if the underlying inspection or qualification event occurred. Do not create a clickable certificate that grants a capability without satisfying requirements.

##### Currency and renewal

- Some qualifications may require periodic currency or refresher training.
- Expired or restricted qualifications should appear clearly in the readiness board.
- Provide renewal or evaluation opportunities through the existing training system.
- Avoid excessive grind. Use appropriate intervals and configurable realism settings.
- Emergency or scenario-specific waivers must be explicit, recorded, and subject to the campaign's rules.


- A pilot certificate is issued only after the relevant existing qualification record is completed.
- An expired qualification changes assignment eligibility only where the scenario requires it.
- An aircraft cannot receive a maintenance release while a blocking defect remains unresolved.
- Certificate history survives save/load and is linked to the personnel or aircraft ID.

**AIRCRAFT DELIVERY, ACCEPTANCE, TRANSFER, AND RETIREMENT CEREMONIES**

existing already includes production, deliveries, ferry flights, replacements, aircraft identity, and service history. This section adds the missing formal lifecycle events and presentation while reusing those systems.


- When an aircraft is produced, purchased, donated, transferred, or released from reserve, create a delivery record linked to the existing procurement and logistics event.
- Track aircraft identity, tail number, origin, destination, receiving unit, delivery method, arrival time, acceptance status, inspection outcome, and any restrictions.
- The aircraft must physically or strategically arrive through the existing ferry, transport, or transfer system before it enters the receiving unit's available inventory.
- Support optional arrival ceremonies, squadron photographs, commander remarks, and news coverage when a character or journalist is present.
- Do not create a ceremonial event if the aircraft was lost, diverted, or never delivered.

##### Transfers and reassignment

- Preserve the aircraft's service identity and history when it changes base, squadron, country, or role.
- Record handover, receiving inspection, configuration changes, maintenance requirements, and support compatibility.
- Reassignment must update the existing authoritative inventory exactly once.

##### Retirement and final disposition

Allow aircraft to leave active service through retirement, write-off, long-term storage, reserve transfer, museum preservation, sale/transfer where scenario-supported, or disposal. The decision can depend on age, accumulated hours, condition, maintenance cost, parts availability, modernization, safety findings, and national policy.

- A retired aircraft cannot be selected for an ordinary sortie unless the scenario explicitly returns it to service and completes the necessary inspection and preparation.
- Preserve its final tail number, service history, notable missions, maintenance record, awards/markings, and reason for retirement.
- Allow a retirement ceremony or historical display when appropriate, but do not require one for every aircraft.
- Keep reserve aircraft distinct from retired aircraft. Reserve assets may return to service; permanently retired assets do not automatically do so.


- A newly delivered aircraft does not enter operational inventory before confirmed arrival and acceptance.
- Transfer does not duplicate the aircraft in two squadrons.
- Retirement removes the aircraft from active readiness while preserving its history.
- A stored reserve aircraft can return only through the existing reactivation and maintenance process.

---

#### Operational history, public information, and campaign consequences
**PLAYER PRESENTATION, BRIEFING, AND INFORMATION QUALITY**

##### Readable status rather than raw simulation noise
Present relevant information at the appropriate level: pilot condition, base readiness, carrier operations, hospital capacity, national policy, coalition restrictions, navigation confidence, maintenance bottlenecks, and event history. Avoid flooding the player with every background event.

##### Explain delays and failures
Whenever a sortie, order, shipment, rescue, repair, or diplomatic request cannot proceed, provide a concise reason and, where possible, a next step. Examples: no qualified crew, spare part unavailable, host-nation approval pending, runway inspection incomplete, destination hospital full, or report confidence insufficient.

##### Decision history
Record important player and AI decisions with time, authority, options considered at a summary level, outcome, and consequences. Do not reveal hidden internal chain-of-thought for AI characters. Provide concise rationale summaries based on visible factors.

##### Briefings and debriefings
Briefings should identify mission purpose, requesting authority, known situation, uncertain information, support, restrictions, expected duration, recovery plan, and possible civilian or diplomatic sensitivity. Debriefings should distinguish confirmed results, estimates, unverified claims, and unresolved questions.

##### Accessibility and localization
Support scalable text, subtitles, color-safe status indicators, keyboard/controller navigation, adjustable information density, configurable units, date/time formats, and language localization. Critical warnings must not rely on color alone.


**SQUADRON NOTICE BOARD AND DAILY UNIT BULLETIN**

existing already defines squadron traditions, recurring characters, event feeds, notifications, and persistent unit histories. Add a focused notice-board interface that assembles relevant items from those systems.

##### Board content

Display relevant items such as:
- Daily orders and approved announcements.
- Upcoming mission and training schedules.
- Deployment and rotation notices.
- Pilot and crew availability changes.
- Maintenance and aircraft availability summaries.
- Promotions, transfers, leave, and qualification notices.
- Commendations, achievements, and memorial announcements.
- Squadron events, anniversaries, ceremonies, and traditions.
- Commander's messages and administrative reminders.
- Relevant campaign news and local base notices.

##### Authorship and delivery

- Each notice has an author/source, publication time, effective time if relevant, audience, priority, and expiration or archive state.
- Notices should be generated from actual events or entered by an authorized character/commander.
- A notice must not be treated as an order unless it carries a valid command authority and order identifier.
- Players can mark notices as read, bookmark them, and open the linked personnel, mission, event, or facility record.
- Avoid repeating the same notice through the board, event feed, and alert center without showing that the entries refer to one underlying event.


- A real promotion or deployment event creates a linked notice.
- Unauthorized players cannot publish command orders.
- Expired notices move to the archive rather than disappearing from history.
- Marking a notice read does not alter campaign state.
