Claude should inspect existing data and implement only missing content. The following are data categories to add where the project does not already support them:

- Pilot physiological profiles, survival kits, medical restrictions, and recovery states.
- Airbase departments, service teams, crew qualifications, shifts, parking slots, runway states, and base alert postures.
- Carrier classes, air wing organization, deck capacity, launch/recovery equipment, shipboard support, and replenishment dependencies.
- CBRN incident types as abstract hazards, detection reports, protective posture, public alerts, response teams, and clearance states.
- Concealment properties, signature categories, decoy archetypes, source reliability, and verification status.
- Navigation source availability, database versions, position confidence, time synchronization, and alternate routing capability.
- Incident evidence, investigations, legal reviews, disciplinary outcomes, civilian harm assessment, and compensation records.
- Coalition membership, national caveats, host-nation agreements, equipment compatibility, translation, and intelligence-sharing tiers.
- Research programs, technology maturity, procurement stages, upgrade packages, export controls, and modernization policies.
- Healthcare facilities, staff capacity, medical supply inventories, public-health alerts, and accessibility needs.
- Government structures, succession rules, cabinet roles, legislative approvals, political factions, and continuity plans.
- Spare-part definitions, platform compatibility, component condition, repair echelons, workforce qualifications, and repair jobs.
- Family links, notification status, memorial events, language/localization, cultural sites, archives, hotlines, research institutions, and industrial emergency records.
- Campaign clock configuration, simulation tiers, recurring schedules, event queue, catch-up rules, and deterministic replay state.
- New mission templates, requesting authorities, mission constraints, support requirements, failure conditions, and debrief templates.

#### Cross-domain dependencies and operational integration contracts
**World simulation governance, policy conflicts, and institutional capacity**

##### Institutional capability
Governments and institutions have jurisdiction, authority, legal mandate, staff, budget, information quality, legitimacy, coordination capacity, and implementation delay.

##### Policy conflicts
Policies can conflict across ministries, levels of government, treaties, courts, and private actors. Record authority and legal status; do not silently apply an impossible policy.

##### Decision process
AI institutions evaluate objectives, constraints, available evidence, budget, political incentives, uncertainty, and implementation capacity. They may make mistakes, but mistakes must be explainable and bounded.

##### Institutional failure and recovery
Institutions can lose capacity through corruption, fiscal stress, displacement, disaster, conflict, or staff loss. Rebuilding requires lawful authority, trained personnel, funding, records, and public trust.


A government announces a policy but fails to implement it due to missing budget or staff. The campaign records the difference between announcement, authorization, implementation, and outcome.

### Additional end-to-end integration scenarios

Add acceptance scenarios for: (1) diplomatic crisis resolved through staged mediation; (2) ceasefire terms proposed, amended, ratified, monitored, and partially violated; (3) command succession after a leader becomes unavailable; (4) explainable order delay; (5) sortie generation constrained by maintenance, crew, fuel, and runway; (6) equipment fault traced through service and repair history; (7) joint operation with dependencies and deconfliction; (8) doctrine change from lesson to adoption; (9) intelligence confidence updated after corroboration; (10) misinformation corrected without rewriting the original report; (11) migration without double-counting; (12) demographic forecast diverging from actual outcomes with assumptions retained; (13) technology diffusion delayed by industrial/training constraints; (14) regional projects competing for finite resources; (15) archives surviving leadership turnover; (16) independent histories disagreeing while citing canonical events; (17) public trust changing after documented failure and investigation; (18) infrastructure outages propagating through dependencies; (19) postwar demobilization/recovery persisting across saves; and (20) multiplayer reconnection restoring exactly-once campaign state.

## 19. Implementation Order and Claude Execution Workflow


### Unified implementation order and Claude execution workflow

#### Single global implementation roadmap and Claude workflow
**Implementation order and Claude execution plan**

##### Phase 0 — repository and document audit

Before editing code:
- inspect the current branch, working tree, script loading order, relevant campaign/sensor/multiplayer systems, and test harness;
- identify all existing authorities, registries, data structures, update loops, save formats, and UI projections;
- map existing source sections to existing files and functions;
- record baseline behavior and run existing tests;
- create the traceability and ownership matrices from Chapter 01.

Do not infer that a feature is absent because its name differs. Search for equivalent behavior before creating anything.

##### Phase 1 — stabilize shared foundations

Audit and establish canonical entity IDs, world coordinate authority, world clock, event contract, save/version contract, multiplayer authority, and diagnostic logging. Resolve duplicate data owners before adding more content. Add migration tests before changing persistent schemas.

##### Phase 2 — prove one vertical slice

Implement one connected vertical slice that uses existing core gameplay. Recommended first slice: one airbase, one playable aircraft, one squadron/personnel set, finite fuel/ammunition, maintenance, one supply route, one mission, one sensor/command context, one mission outcome, and a persistent debrief/history record. Demonstrate that all views and counters refer to the same IDs and events.

##### Phase 3 — connect the military enterprise

Unify order of battle, personnel, equipment, readiness, maintenance, procurement, training, logistics, airbase/carrier/port operations, and force accounting. Add ground/naval elements through shared contracts and domain-specific capabilities. Re-run all aircraft and campaign regressions at each step.

##### Phase 4 — connect geography and infrastructure

Stabilize geographic authority, streamed world layers, transport networks, settlements, airports/ports, utilities, energy, water, construction, and asset condition. Keep rendering LOD separate from persistent simulation state.

##### Phase 5 — connect the global economy

Integrate resources, materials, producers, trade, workforce, households, public finance, banking, insurance, and consumption. Start with a limited, testable supply chain and scale after accounting reconciles.

##### Phase 6 — connect people and institutions

Integrate households, population, migration, employment, education, health, disability, community services, local government, courts, media, cultural institutions, and international organizations. Use aggregate simulation where individual detail is unnecessary.

##### Phase 7 — connect environment, hazards, and response

Integrate weather, climate, ecology, hazard/incident generation, emergency services, humanitarian response, recovery, and resilience through the shared incident and event contracts.

##### Phase 8 — integrate autonomous AI and historical development

Add institution-specific decisions, planning horizons, learning, autonomous national development, and multi-decade continuity only after the shared time, event, capacity, and audit foundations are stable.

##### Phase 9 — unify player presentation and end-to-end campaign flows

Connect maps, dashboards, mission generation, briefings, debriefings, player career, awards, multiplayer, anti-war consequences, endings, memorials, and postwar continuation to canonical read models. Chapter 14 remains authoritative for anti-war presentation.

##### Phase 10 — performance, scale, and release

Test representative low-, medium-, and high-end hardware. Stress active tactical areas, multiple theaters, large populations, event archives, long histories, multiplayer reconnect, save migration, map streaming, and long-duration campaign simulation. Apply measured budgets and bounded fallbacks. Do not claim whole-Earth full-detail simulation.

##### Claude work cadence

For each phase:
1. State the existing files and systems found.
2. State the canonical owner and interfaces selected.
3. Identify what will be reused, extended, or newly added.
4. Implement one vertical slice.
5. Run targeted tests and core regression tests.
6. Inspect runtime behavior and logs.
7. Report remaining gaps and deferred items.
8. Update traceability and ownership matrices.
9. Commit only a coherent, testable change when instructed by the repository workflow.

Never implement every domain in one enormous unreviewed code change. Never report a feature complete because a data structure or UI mockup exists; its lifecycle, persistence, interactions, tests, and failure behavior must work.

## 20. Acceptance Criteria, Regression, Data Integrity, Performance, and Release Gates


### Unified acceptance, regression, data integrity, performance, and release framework

#### Quality assurance, acceptance, regression, performance, and release integrity
**Testing and edge cases**

- Test an individual surrender, a flight surrender, a surrounded unit surrender, a city handover, and a country-level capitulation.
- Test a surrender signal that is misidentified, a surrender request that is never accepted, a unit that does not receive the ceasefire order, and a local commander who refuses a national agreement.
- Test a country that surrenders while its allies continue fighting, a coalition member that leaves the war, and a non-state group that refuses the peace agreement.
- Test negotiations that succeed, fail, pause, restart after a leadership change, or produce only a local humanitarian agreement.
- Test ceasefire violations, disputed attribution, neutral observers, buffer zones, expiration dates, renewal, and a frozen conflict that later resumes.
- Test save/load during negotiations, during a surrender process, immediately after a treaty is signed, and during postwar reconstruction.
- Verify that a recognized surrender prevents further attacks by compliant AI units and that all ceasefire rules are applied consistently across player and AI forces.
- Verify that the player can understand why a peace proposal was accepted or rejected and why the campaign ended in its particular state.


**Unified acceptance and regression catalogue for all campaign and flight systems**

##### Core game preservation

All existing flight controls, flight dynamics, aircraft, cockpits, avionics, radars/sensors, weapons, missions, campaign behavior, multiplayer flow, and current supported browser workflows remain functional. No excluded navigation aid/procedure or world editor is introduced.

##### One-world integrity

Every persistent entity and event has stable identity, owner, location where applicable, lifecycle, provenance, and authority. Streaming, rendering changes, time acceleration, save migration, replay, reconnect, and host migration do not duplicate or erase canonical state.

##### Economic and military accounting

Personnel, force strength, platform counts, ammunition, fuel, inventory, production, shipment, finance, costs, and losses reconcile under documented rules. No unlimited resource creation, hidden double counting, or untraceable disappearance.

##### Human and civilian integrity

Population, household, migration, injury, disability, death, missing status, displacement, health, public services, family, and postwar records reconcile. Civilian harm is never a reward or spectacle. Chapter 14 evidence, privacy, dignity, uncertainty, accountability, and anti-war requirements are mandatory.

##### Simulation integrity

The simulation is deterministic or replayable where authoritative outcomes require it. Random outcomes are seeded or recorded. Causal loops are bounded. AI respects information, authority, capacity, and resources. Offline progression is represented honestly.

##### Geographic and rendering integrity

The global world is spatially coherent, with streaming and LOD. Persistent entities survive tile unloads. Global, regional, local, and tactical views refer to the same world state. Rendering complexity remains bounded by measured device capability.

##### Multiplayer and security

Authority, permissions, transaction integrity, validation, recovery, reconnect, and host migration tests pass. No client can forge authoritative inventory, finances, casualties, mission outcomes, or campaign history.

##### Observability and explainability

Important state changes and displayed metrics can be traced to authoritative source records. Diagnostics identify broken references, duplicate entities, invalid transitions, performance bottlenecks, and inconsistent projections.

##### Content and data quality

Country, equipment, infrastructure, population, and geographic data have source, license, attribution, date, confidence, and scenario relevance. Do not present unsupported estimates as verified facts. Missing coverage has a documented fallback.

##### Release definition

The consolidated specification is satisfied only when:
- all retained requirements are mapped to code, tests, or explicit deferrals;
- shared authorities and data contracts are documented;
- representative end-to-end scenarios in Chapter 18 pass;
- core game regression tests pass;
- save/load, export/import, migration, replay, and multiplayer recovery pass;
- performance is measured and remains within declared budgets on the target hardware set;
- no duplicate managers or conflicting sources of truth remain;
- Chapter 14 remains the sole consolidated anti-war implementation contract;
- the implementation report distinguishes implemented, partial, deferred, and unsupported features honestly.

**Integrated subsystem regression and end-to-end acceptance tests.**

- The player can see an AWACS mission orbit on the strategic map; when the aircraft returns to base, its coverage gap becomes visible.
- A drone can launch, perform reconnaissance, report uncertain contacts, lose communications, return or be lost, and affect campaign intelligence.
- A cargo aircraft receives a real supply request, loads a finite cargo manifest, delivers it to a compatible active airfield, and updates destination inventories.
- A damaged or closed runway prevents an incompatible cargo aircraft from landing; the AI diverts or cancels appropriately.
- A tanker has finite fuel transfer capacity and must rotate, refuel, and undergo maintenance.
- A SAM battery has separate radar, command, launcher, ammunition, and support states; destroying one component does not incorrectly erase every other component.
- A mobile SAM can relocate and consume time/fuel/supply; a fixed radar site cannot move.
- A battery with empty interceptors requests reload and cannot continue firing as if ammunition were unlimited.
- A supply convoy can be delayed, rerouted, damaged, or lost; dependent units then experience real shortages.
- A recovery vehicle can retrieve a disabled vehicle only if it has capacity, access, and a valid route.
- A medical evacuation request can be queued, assigned, delayed, diverted, or denied when all assets or hospitals are occupied.
- A naval group must receive replenishment to sustain extended deployment; a damaged port changes its available options.
- Country and year filters prevent an unfielded prototype from appearing as a normal operational unit in an earlier campaign.
- Existing fighter aircraft, player controls, cockpit systems, and aircraft data remain unchanged after the new systems are added.


Claude must implement and test complete examples, not just create empty classes or UI placeholders.

##### Combat medic tests
1. An AI infantry unit takes casualties. Its medic identifies the wounded personnel, provides treatment within available supplies, and reports the casualty state to command.
2. Two casualties require attention at the same time. The medic uses the configured triage priority and does not treat both simultaneously if the simulation says only one can be treated at a time.
3. A medic runs out of medical supplies. The unit reports the shortage and requests resupply; the medic does not continue using unlimited items.
4. A casualty is loaded into an available ambulance or evacuation vehicle, transported to a facility with capacity, treated, and given a persistent recovery outcome.
5. A hospital becomes unavailable or full. The medical AI searches for another suitable destination or reports that evacuation is delayed.
6. A medic becomes wounded or is separated from the unit. The unit's medical capability changes and the command system reflects it.
7. A medical facility is damaged or isolated. Capacity and access change, civilian and military patients are affected, and news or diplomatic consequences appear only when the event becomes known.

##### War reporter and news tests
1. A reporter embedded with a unit witnesses a real campaign event and records a clip connected to the correct event ID, location, time, and camera position.
2. A reporter who is too far away or has no line of sight cannot create footage showing details they could not have observed.
3. The clip passes through transfer, review, verification, editing, and publication states and then appears in the existing news interface.
4. The player opens the news story and sees the actual captured clip, replay sequence, stills, or clearly labeled simulated summary.
5. A communications outage delays the publication without deleting the captured footage.
6. Two outlets report the same event differently while preserving the distinction between verified facts, claims, and editorial framing.
7. A reporter is evacuated from a dangerous area. The reporter's assignment, footage, status, and employer are saved and restored correctly.
8. A major event with no nearby reporters does not automatically receive invented video coverage. It may appear later through another credible source.

##### Pilot rescue tests
1. The player's aircraft is lost and the player ejects successfully. The player enters downed-pilot mode with the correct pilot identity, mission, location estimate, equipment, and campaign state.
2. The player activates a beacon. Friendly command receives a report with realistic uncertainty and the rescue mission generator evaluates available assets.
3. The nearest rescue asset is unavailable. The command system chooses another option, delays the mission, or reports that no suitable rescue is currently possible.
4. A rescue team reaches the search area but does not immediately know the pilot's exact location. It must use available clues and observations to locate them.
5. The player is recovered. The same pilot identity returns to the campaign and enters the medical treatment and recovery system.
6. The player is captured before friendly forces arrive. The pilot is marked captured—not dead or merely missing—and enters the prisoner system.
7. An AI pilot ejects. The same search, rescue, capture, medical, and persistence rules apply without player-only shortcuts.
8. A pilot remains missing after an unsuccessful search. The campaign records the unresolved status and can generate later intelligence or search events.
9. A successful rescue is reported by a journalist only if the reporter or a credible source actually has access to the event.
10. Save and reload during a rescue. The downed pilot, search area, assigned assets, communications, medical state, footage, and mission progress persist without duplication.


Claude must demonstrate these complete end-to-end tests:

1. **Normal communications:** A player order is sent through a friendly network, delivered to the correct unit, acknowledged, and recorded in the campaign event history.
2. **Localized jamming:** A fictionalized jammer degrades a selected network in a limited area. Units outside the affected area remain unaffected unless another simulated cause applies.
3. **Different network effects:** Jamming one tactical network does not automatically disable every command, emergency, civilian, and data network in the theater.
4. **Message delay:** A report created during degraded communications arrives later with its original timestamp and a clear indication that it may be stale.
5. **No acknowledgement:** A player issues an order, but the recipient does not receive it. The interface shows that delivery failed or remains unconfirmed rather than falsely reporting success.
6. **AI fallback:** A ground formation loses contact with headquarters and continues under its last verified orders, uses local initiative within its authority, and seeks a fallback communication path when appropriate.
7. **Radio silence:** A unit under radio-silence orders limits routine transmissions but continues to function, navigate, defend itself, and perform its mission.
8. **Interception detection:** An enemy intelligence asset collects an eligible transmission and creates a time-stamped intelligence report with confidence and uncertainty.
9. **Content uncertainty:** A collected signal does not automatically reveal exact message content, the sender's exact location, and the full operational plan. The available intelligence must match the simulation's security and collection rules.
10. **Direction-finding uncertainty:** A location estimate is an area with confidence and age, not an always-perfect live marker. A moving unit can leave the estimated area before the report is used.
11. **Intelligence fusion:** Analysts combine radio-derived information with other sources and produce an assessment that distinguishes confirmed facts from inference.
12. **Spoofed order:** An invalid or suspicious order is challenged, checked, or rejected by an AI unit when its authority and security rules require verification.
13. **Relay recovery:** A unit restores communications through an available relay and sends queued reports without duplicating or incorrectly refreshing their original timestamps.
14. **AWACS or relay loss:** Losing an airborne relay reduces the relevant communications coverage, while unaffected networks continue operating.
15. **Drone link loss:** A drone follows its configured lost-link behavior rather than freezing, teleporting, or remaining under perfect remote control.
16. **Rescue under jamming:** A pilot-rescue mission experiences a communications problem, uses a fallback method or alternate relay where available, and preserves the pilot's actual location uncertainty.
17. **Medevac under jamming:** Medical staff can still act locally. Command may receive the request late, and the evacuation outcome reflects actual availability and timing.
18. **Civilian communication impact:** A major outage affects selected emergency or public-information services and creates plausible campaign consequences without automatically disabling every civilian service.
19. **News footage transfer:** A reporter records a clip while disconnected. The clip remains locally stored and is transferred only after a valid communications path becomes available.
20. **Save/load persistence:** Save during a jamming event with queued messages and an interception report. Reload and verify that message state, intelligence, jamming duration, and unit behavior persist without duplication.
21. **Faction separation:** Bluefor cannot automatically read Redfor's intercepted communications, and Redfor cannot automatically read Bluefor's. Information must be collected, shared, or otherwise acquired through the simulation.
22. **Performance:** Run many units and networks across distant campaign regions. Background networks update efficiently without losing important state transitions or flooding the event queue.
23. **Player clarity:** The player can tell whether a message was sent, received, acknowledged, delayed, jammed, or rejected. Important failures are explainable without revealing hidden enemy intelligence.
24. **Difficulty controls:** Changing communication realism settings changes the intended difficulty variables without corrupting campaign saves or silently changing faction capabilities.


Claude must add automated or repeatable tests for at least the following:

1. **World seed stability:** Start a campaign, save, reload, and confirm generated geography and settlement positions remain identical.
2. **Chunk persistence:** Damage a structure, unload its chunk, reload it, and confirm the damage remains.
3. **Ownership consistency:** Capture a base and confirm map ownership, logistics access, mission generation, and AI control all agree.
4. **Unit identity:** Move a unit across several regions and confirm its identifier, history, personnel, and inventory remain intact.
5. **Supply accounting:** Deliver fuel and confirm the source inventory decreases, the transport carries the amount, and the destination receives the same amount.
6. **Supply route failure:** Close a bridge and confirm logistics recalculates or reports that no valid route exists.
7. **Production:** Queue equipment production, advance campaign time, and confirm resources are consumed and equipment becomes available only after completion.
8. **Maintenance:** Damage a support unit, assign repair, consume parts, and confirm readiness changes gradually.
9. **Airbase capacity:** Fill parking, fuel, or maintenance capacity and confirm additional operations are delayed or diverted.
10. **Airspace deconfliction:** Create overlapping friendly operations and verify the airspace manager handles them through scheduling, routing, or warnings.
11. **AI uncertainty:** Hide an enemy unit from a faction and verify its AI does not plan around the exact hidden location.
12. **Intelligence age:** Advance time without new collection and confirm track confidence or freshness changes according to its source.
13. **Communications failure:** Jam a network and verify only affected message paths are degraded.
14. **AI fallback:** Disconnect a unit from headquarters and confirm it continues under valid last orders.
15. **AI retreat:** Create an untenable unit state and verify it can request support, withdraw, reorganize, surrender, or choose another plausible response.
16. **Medical request:** Create casualties and verify a medic or medical unit receives a request and uses available capacity.
17. **Player rescue:** Eject the player, create a rescue state, launch a rescue mission, complete recovery, and verify the player's career and injury state persist.
18. **Capture:** Capture a named character and confirm they are removed from active command and unit assignment.
19. **News footage:** Generate an observable event and confirm a nearby reporter can record it, transfer it, verify it, and publish a clip.
20. **News uncertainty:** Create a disputed event and confirm the news interface distinguishes confirmed information from an unverified report.
21. **Civilian services:** Damage a utility facility and verify only dependent regions or services are affected according to the network model.
22. **Humanitarian relief:** Deliver aid and verify distribution and population outcomes rather than only cargo arrival.
23. **Diplomatic restriction:** Revoke an overflight or basing permission and verify the AI respects the change and replans.
24. **Coalition independence:** Make two allies disagree about an operation and verify one does not automatically inherit the other's decision.
25. **Proxy independence:** Make a sponsor change policy and verify a proxy group can disagree or behave independently within its state.
26. **Ceasefire:** Sign a ceasefire and verify compliant forces stop initiating combat while disputed or non-signatory actors remain separately represented.
27. **Surrender:** Have a unit surrender and verify it enters a protected prisoner state and no longer receives combat orders.
28. **Peace treaty:** Complete negotiations and verify campaign status, borders, military restrictions, prisoners, and postwar tasks update coherently.
29. **Save migration:** Load an older save and verify the migration process either succeeds safely or reports exactly why it cannot.
30. **Long-duration simulation:** Advance a campaign through an extended period and check for duplicate entities, impossible inventory, stale missions, event floods, and performance degradation.
31. **Multi-theater isolation:** Change one theater and verify unrelated theaters update only when affected by shared logistics, diplomacy, or strategic events.
32. **Performance degradation:** Increase entity count and verify the simulation lowers distant detail before breaking critical world-state correctness.
33. **Faction information separation:** Confirm one faction cannot read another's private intelligence, command messages, or inventory without an acquisition or sharing event.
34. **Campaign restart:** Start a new campaign and confirm no state from the previous campaign leaks into the new one.
35. **Player disconnect:** In multiplayer, disconnect a player and verify their assigned role transitions safely to an AI or fallback state.


Claude must implement and test the following behaviors:

1. **Oil-to-fuel chain:** Produce crude at an oil field, transport it to a refinery, refine it, move the resulting product to a depot, and deliver it to an airbase. Verify each inventory changes exactly once.
2. **Refinery outage:** Reduce refinery capacity and confirm finished-product output falls after available stocks are accounted for.
3. **Crude shortage:** Remove crude supply and confirm the refinery consumes remaining feedstock before reducing throughput.
4. **Power outage:** Remove grid power from a refinery and verify it enters an appropriate reduced or shutdown state.
5. **Pipeline interruption:** Make a route unavailable and verify shipments stop, reroute, or report a blocker.
6. **Storage full:** Fill a destination tank and confirm incoming shipments wait, divert, or are rejected safely without inventory duplication.
7. **Airport fuel shortage:** Reduce aviation-fuel inventory and confirm sortie generation and refueling capacity respond accordingly.
8. **Ground-unit fuel shortage:** Reduce a formation's fuel and confirm it changes its movement and mission behavior.
9. **Naval fuel endurance:** Advance a ship's operations and verify fuel state, endurance, and return planning remain consistent.
10. **Civilian allocation:** Prioritize military consumption and confirm civilian transport or industrial services experience gradual, explainable effects.
11. **Strategic reserve release:** Release reserve stocks and verify availability increases while the strategic reserve decreases.
12. **International trade:** Import fuel from a partner and verify contracts, shipment movement, border/port permissions, and arrival inventory.
13. **Sanctions or export restriction:** Change a trade permission and verify affected shipments are blocked or renegotiated rather than teleporting to the destination.
14. **Offshore weather:** Apply severe weather and verify offshore production or transport is delayed according to configured limits.
15. **Restoration:** Repair a damaged facility using resources and time, and verify capacity returns progressively or after required testing.
16. **Environmental response:** Create an industrial incident and verify emergency services, cleanup, affected population, and recovery status update.
17. **AI fuel planning:** Give a commander an operation whose known fuel requirement exceeds available supply and verify it delays, scales down, or finds a valid alternative.
18. **Faction knowledge:** Verify an AI faction cannot access a rival's hidden inventory or future shipment information without a valid intelligence source.
19. **Campaign generation:** Start multiple seeded campaigns and verify resource distributions vary while map and network constraints remain coherent.
20. **Save and reload:** Save a shipment in transit, reload, and confirm its position, cargo, and expected delivery persist without duplication.

A feature is not complete because a menu, icon, counter, or data object exists. It is complete only when its actual behavior is connected to campaign state, its lifecycle works, and its failure paths are handled.

For each implemented subsystem, report:
- What files and APIs were inspected.
- What existing implementation was reused or reworked.
- What new behavior was added.
- What data model and event types were changed.
- What scripts were added or changed and where they are loaded.
- Which existing features were regression-tested.
- Which new acceptance tests passed or failed.
- Whether save/load and multiplayer behavior were tested.
- Performance measurements where relevant.
- Any limitations, approximations, or remaining placeholders.

##### No fake completion

Do not claim success if a feature is only represented by a button, static value, placeholder model, scripted message, or hardcoded counter. Clearly label partial features. Do not invent test results.

##### No unnecessary broad rewrite

Keep the implementation incremental. If a large refactor is necessary, split it into safe extractions with a boot and regression test after each stage. Do not replace the entire campaign, `game.js`, or multiplayer system in one unreviewed pass.

##### Preserve the player's existing content

Do not erase existing campaigns, flight records, aircraft, loadouts, controls, settings, or multiplayer compatibility without a migration or clear warning. Back up save data before schema migrations.

##### Final objective

Turn the existing browser-based flight game into a much deeper persistent combined-arms campaign while retaining its identity as a flight simulator. The player should be able to fly an existing aircraft while the wider world continues to run at the correct simulation scale; support aircraft and ground formations should perform meaningful work; logistics and persistence should be real; multiplayer should share one coherent campaign; and the statistics, maps, event feed, and history should show what actually happened.

**existing final instruction:** Rework the systems the game already has, add the missing support and campaign systems, and connect them through one consistent browser-friendly simulation architecture. Do not skip existing features, do not duplicate them, do not replace the game engine, and do not introduce fake functionality. Keep all existing campaign interface requirements, including the explicit exclusion of custom in-flight HUD layouts.

**Performance budgets, stress testing, and scale verification**

##### Performance budget document

Create a performance budget for at least three target classes:
- minimum supported desktop/laptop;
- recommended desktop/laptop;
- high-performance desktop.

Add mobile/tablet only if the project explicitly supports them. Measure real target hardware; do not invent universal FPS guarantees.

For each class, define and test:
- initial load and time to interactive;
- time to first playable flight;
- time to first useful global map;
- region/tile load latency;
- frame-time percentiles, not just average FPS;
- main-thread long tasks;
- JavaScript heap and peak memory;
- GPU memory where measurable;
- draw calls, triangles, visible objects, and texture counts;
- worker count and worker memory;
- active entity count by simulation tier;
- AI/pathfinding jobs per interval;
- event queue depth and processing latency;
- IndexedDB read/write latency and save size;
- network message rate, payload size, and reconnect duration;
- asset download/decode/upload time;
- recovery time after context loss or worker failure.

##### Simulation budgets

Every simulation tier must have explicit:
- maximum active entities;
- update frequency;
- allowed AI decision frequency;
- pathfinding budget;
- event processing budget;
- rendering detail;
- persistence policy;
- promotion/demotion rules.

When budgets are exceeded, degrade distant detail first. Never silently stop processing authoritative events or discard player-visible state. Use back-pressure, queue limits, prioritization, and graceful reduced fidelity.

##### Stress and soak scenarios

Create repeatable tests for:
- a dense city with civilian and military activity;
- multiple active fronts;
- large air operations and support flights;
- large infantry and vehicle populations;
- major weather and environmental effects;
- high wreckage/damage counts;
- long-range global map browsing;
- repeated tactical-region streaming;
- multiplayer with multiple clients and reconnects;
- long campaigns with many historical events;
- storage pressure and save migration;
- worker and WebGL failures.

##### Acceptance gates

- Every supported hardware class has measured baselines and documented results.
- No release claim is made from a single average-FPS measurement.
- Memory and resource counts stabilize during repeated region transitions.
- The campaign remains logically correct when visual quality is reduced.
- Distant simulation load is bounded and observable.
- Performance regressions are tied to a reproducible test scenario.



**Diagnostics, data integrity, migration, and release governance**

##### Unified diagnostics

Add developer diagnostics for:
- canonical campaign time and event sequence;
- entity counts by type and simulation tier;
- country/region/ownership state;
- resource stockpile reconciliation;
- sensor/track confidence and freshness;
- navigation queues and failed routes;
- asset streaming queue and residency;
- memory/resource estimates;
- save/load/migration status;
- multiplayer authority, connection, and replication state;
- worker health and error queues;
- event provenance and rejected commands.

Diagnostics must be opt-in or developer-only where they reveal hidden campaign state.

##### Test pyramid

Require:
- unit tests for pure data transformations and state transitions;
- integration tests for campaign systems sharing authoritative records;
- save/load and migration tests;
- multiplayer command-validation and reconnect tests;
- browser end-to-end tests for critical player journeys;
- deterministic simulation tests where deterministic behavior is claimed;
- performance and soak tests;
- regression tests for the existing flight simulator.

Do not claim a feature is complete because its menu opens. Every feature needs state-based acceptance criteria.

##### Data integrity invariants

Add automated checks for:
- duplicate IDs and broken references;
- impossible lifecycle transitions;
- negative or duplicated inventory;
- resource creation without an authoritative source event;
- dead/captured/missing characters appearing in active rosters incorrectly;
- unit ownership conflicts;
- country and region references that no longer exist;
- campaign time moving backward;
- event replay duplication;
- weapon/munition incompatibility;
- source/provenance gaps;
- save records referencing deleted assets or invalid versions.

##### Release and migration governance

- Maintain a versioned change log and migration tests.
- Run a pre-release data validation report.
- Separate development/debug data from shipped scenario content.
- Document known limitations and unsupported hardware.
- Verify asset/data licenses before distribution.
- Provide a clean new-campaign test and an upgraded-save test.
- Do not merge large content batches without a playable vertical-slice regression run.


##### Final release gate

- all new sections have repository traceability to actual files/functions/tests;
- every relevant requirement is marked implemented, partial, missing, blocked, or not applicable;
- the first geographic vertical slice passes;
- the multiplayer vertical slice passes;
- save/recovery and long-campaign tests pass;
- performance budgets have measured results on stated target hardware;
- existing flight, aircraft, cockpit, avionics, controls, missions, and campaign regressions pass;
- source and asset licensing is reviewed;
- the ending screen and quote archive pass content, accessibility, attribution, and data-integrity tests;
- all limitations and unverified national/geographic data are disclosed.

**Preservation statement:** existing retains all existing content and adds Chapters 03, 04, 06, 12, 13, 14, 16 and 20. It does not claim that every real-world country, asset, weapon, person, road, or building has been exhaustively verified. The objective is a coherent, maintainable, evidence-aware, performant campaign simulation whose detail is bounded by the browser and whose ending remembers the human consequences of war.

- civilian and military consequences are separately reported;
- quote attribution and rights status are reviewed;
- all previous flight simulator and campaign regression tests pass.

**Preservation statement:** existing retains existing and all earlier archived content. It adds Chapters 14 and 20. The destruction ledger is a historical accounting system, not a scoring system. The epilogue exists to remember the people, places, and consequences of the simulated war.


##### General quality gates

A feature is not complete because it has a screen, static sample data, or a counter. It is complete only when it:
- reads and writes authoritative campaign state through documented interfaces;
- has stable IDs and validated lifecycle transitions;
- survives save/load and supported migration;
- respects multiplayer authority and access permissions;
- produces auditable events;
- handles missing, stale, uncertain, and disputed information;
- has deterministic tests for important state transitions;
- integrates with existing campaign and flight systems;
- stays within measured performance and memory budgets;
- passes existing regression tests.

##### Stress and performance tests

Test at increasing campaign scales, not just one hand-built scene:
- many countries and government records;
- thousands of formations/units at strategic abstraction;
- large numbers of shipments and inventory transactions;
- years of weather forecasts and observations;
- large intelligence report histories;
- multiple active emergencies;
- dense port and trade networks;
- long event archives with corrections and snapshots;
- concurrent multiplayer clients with reconnect and host migration.

Measure:
- frame time and update cost by subsystem;
- memory use and garbage collection;
- save/load duration and serialized size;
- event queue backlog;
- archive query latency;
- network bytes and synchronization frequency;
- worker utilization and main-thread stalls;
- map rendering and entity streaming cost.

Do not promise a fixed FPS without target hardware and measurement. Use geographic chunks, LOD, instancing, culling, pooling, workers, IndexedDB where appropriate, pagination, caching, and adaptive simulation frequency. Distant systems must not update at tactical frequency.

##### Determinism and audit tests

- Same seed, same saved state, same simulation steps produce the same deterministic results where determinism is required.
- Event replay is idempotent.
- Duplicate network messages do not duplicate orders, shipments, casualties, or inventory transactions.
- Host migration preserves authoritative command, logistics, and political state.
- Clients cannot edit hidden intelligence, ownership, stock, or office-holder records.
- Archive projections reconcile with current campaign truth and historical snapshots.
- Corrected records retain their original source and correction chain.
- Uncertain estimates remain labeled as estimates.
- Missing telemetry is surfaced, not silently filled with invented data.

##### Regression protection

Before and after each vertical slice, run the existing headless browser test workflow and the project's actual regression suite. Include:
- startup and load;
- aircraft selection and flight;
- flight physics and controls;
- cockpit and existing avionics;
- existing sensor/radar/AWACS/IRST/jamming/SEAD behavior;
- weapons and ammunition accounting;
- missions and campaign progression;
- map and airfield ownership;
- ground and naval units;
- carrier operations and aerial refueling;
- CSAR, personnel, capture, and casualty state;
- save/export/import and migration;
- cooperative multiplayer, reconnect, and host migration;
- end-of-war epilogue, cemetery, and destruction ledger.

Do not weaken or delete tests merely to make the new systems pass.

##### Release criteria

existing may be called integrated only when:
1. All nine systems have at least one working vertical slice.
2. No user-facing world editor or scenario editor has been added.
3. No duplicate country, person, unit, sensor, inventory, weather, event, or map authority has been introduced.
4. Logistics transactions reconcile with Chapter 14 destruction and expenditure ledger ammunition and expenditure accounting.
5. Intelligence respects the existing sensor baseline and information permissions.
6. Bases, ports, and installations reuse existing infrastructure and entity identities.
7. Political changes preserve country identity, diplomacy, and historical records.
8. Emergencies use existing population, infrastructure, finance, logistics, and recovery systems.
9. The historical archive reconciles with campaign events, the epilogue, cemetery, and entity timelines.
10. Save migration, multiplayer authority, deterministic tests, performance profiling, and flight regression gates pass.
11. All uncertainty, missing data, and generated fictional records are labeled honestly.
12. No new feature turns civilian harm, disaster losses, or destruction into rewards.


##### Required functional tests

At minimum, prove:
- one full supplier-to-customer economic transaction;
- production limited by actual input and capacity;
- inventory reconciliation;
- shipment and payment lifecycle;
- price and household affordability response;
- business liquidity and insolvency state;
- government budget and procurement reconciliation;
- insurance claim and payout lifecycle;
- one infrastructure disruption with downstream effects;
- one healthcare supply and service-capacity response;
- one school/workforce/training response;
- one civilian transport disruption;
- one airline/airport/airspace disruption;
- one satellite service outage and recovery;
- one research program lifecycle;
- one environmental incident and restoration project;
- one international organization aid program;
- one treaty declaration, verification, dispute, and consultation sequence;
- one heritage institution damage and restoration sequence;
- one long-term reconstruction project.

##### Economic integrity tests

- Every inventory has a reconciled opening and closing balance.
- Production cannot exceed available capacity and inputs.
- Transfers do not create new goods.
- Shipments are counted once.
- Contracts, invoices, payments, and deliveries are separate states.
- Loans, repayments, defaults, and write-offs reconcile.
- Government budgets distinguish appropriation, commitment, expenditure, and payment.
- Currency conversion is historically stable.
- Historical price indices do not rewrite old transactions.
- Business closure preserves liabilities, employees, and records.
- Reconstruction cannot exceed available funding, labor, material, and transport.
- Dashboards match ledger-derived totals within documented rounding rules.

##### Cross-system tests

Run controlled causal scenarios:
1. Port disruption affecting trade, manufacturing, employment, prices, public revenue, and reconstruction.
2. Energy disruption affecting utilities, hospitals, rail, data centers, and industry with different backup capacity.
3. Workforce shortage affecting healthcare, education, construction, and transport.
4. Public-health emergency affecting service demand, workforce availability, household spending, and government budgets.
5. Environmental contamination affecting water, agriculture, health, insurance, and remediation.
6. Satellite communications outage affecting only dependent services and users.
7. Treaty dispute affecting diplomatic status and confidence without automatically starting a war.
8. International aid pledge that does not count as delivered until funded, transported, and received.
9. Airport closure affecting airline schedules, passenger mobility, cargo, and company finances.
10. Reconstruction project competing with ordinary industry for labor, materials, credit, and transport.

##### Performance and scale

Measure:
- strategic tick time by subsystem;
- regional tick time;
- event queue backlog;
- dependency graph traversal cost;
- economic ledger size;
- save/load duration and size;
- IndexedDB usage;
- memory and garbage collection;
- worker utilization;
- UI dashboard query latency;
- network bytes and synchronization;
- multiplayer reconciliation time.

Test with many countries, regions, companies, institutions, transactions, shipments, people cohorts, satellites, and years of history. Use aggregation and pagination. Do not promise fixed FPS without target hardware and measurement.

##### Determinism and resilience

- Same seed, same saved state, and same ordered simulation steps produce the same results where deterministic behavior is required.
- Event replay is idempotent.
- Duplicate network messages do not duplicate money, goods, casualties, deliveries, or contracts.
- Host migration preserves economic and institutional authority.
- Stale clients cannot overwrite newer ledgers.
- Interrupted saves recover without partial financial transactions.
- existing saves migrate without fabricated historical records.
- Unknown data remains explicitly unknown.
- Forecasts and estimates remain distinguishable from observations.

Run the existing headless browser workflow and all available project tests. Preserve regression coverage for:
- startup and loading;

- carriers and aerial refueling;

Do not weaken or delete tests to make existing pass.

##### Mandatory integration scenarios

At minimum, implement and test these complete chains:

1. **Drought-to-household chain:** climate trend → weather event → water availability → agriculture → food processing → logistics → retail → household affordability → public assistance → adaptation investment.
2. **City-growth chain:** employer investment → jobs → migration/commuting → housing demand → construction → utility demand → transport demand → municipal budgets → public services.
3. **Energy-transition chain:** policy → funding → research/workforce → project construction → grid connection → energy supply/prices → industry and household effects → emissions/environment indicators.
4. **Digital-outage chain:** infrastructure failure → dependent services → payments/logistics/healthcare disruption → business and household effects → restoration investment.
5. **Housing-finance chain:** interest/credit conditions → construction finance → housing supply → rents/ownership → household affordability → migration and municipal revenue.
6. **Climate-adaptation chain:** hazard/exposure assessment → public budget → project procurement → labor/material demand → construction → reduced risk → measured outcomes.
7. **Legal-enforcement chain:** complaint/allegation → investigation → hearing/decision → appeal/enforcement → company/property/contract state → finance and public trust.
8. **Municipal-sanitation chain:** waste generation → collection capacity → treatment/disposal → environmental indicators → public health → municipal costs and service response.
9. **Demographic chain:** aging/migration → workforce and enrollment → pensions and healthcare → public budgets → policy changes → household effects.
10. **Integrity chain:** procurement irregularity → audit → investigation → legal outcome → project delay/cost → reconstruction and institutional trust.
11. **Tourism chain:** environmental or security disruption → travel demand → accommodation/transport → employment and revenue → public finances → recovery and visitor confidence.
12. **Peaceful-development chain:** scientific investment → education and skills → business formation → employment → city growth → trade → tax revenue → further investment.

##### Cross-system correctness tests

- Every major interaction follows a valid dependency edge.
- Every derived change has source-event traceability.
- Events are ordered and idempotent.
- Cycles do not cause unbounded repeated updates.
- Physical quantities, money, people, and ownership reconcile.
- Local failures remain geographically bounded unless a real network dependency propagates them.
- Backup systems and alternatives are represented.
- Policies require authority, funding, and implementation capacity.
- Delayed effects are not applied instantly.
- Forecasts and estimates do not become historical facts.
- AI does not use hidden information or exceed authority.
- Content packs cannot bypass validation or permissions.

Use aggregation, batching, caching, geographic partitions, workers, and bounded histories. Do not update every city, farm, household, company, or network node every render frame. Do not promise a fixed frame rate without target hardware and measurement.

##### Mandatory regression suite
Run existing tests and preserve behavior for:
- aircraft and flight physics;
- cockpits, avionics, controls, and existing aircraft;
- ground forces, maritime forces, carriers, and aerial refueling;
- economy, logistics, trade, finance, and industry;
- save/export/import and migration;

##### Data integrity gates
All authoritative entities and events require stable IDs. No duplicate transaction, double-spend, duplicate casualty, orphaned reference, invalid ownership, impossible negative inventory, or unexplained resource creation is permitted. Every derived value must be traceable to source records and rules.

##### Performance gates
Measure on defined target hardware and browsers. Record CPU time, frame time, GPU memory, system memory, draw calls, active objects, tile load latency, cache hit rate, worker utilization, save size, event replay time, and multiplayer bandwidth. Use budgets established from baseline profiling; do not invent universal FPS guarantees.

##### Scale tests
Test:
- global map with all country boundaries and generalized terrain;
- long-distance flight with repeated tile streaming;
- dense city local-detail activation and eviction;
- multiple simultaneous regional crises;
- multi-decade campaign advancement;
- large event history with bounded archival;
- multiplayer concurrency and reconnect;
- save migration from existing and earlier supported versions.

A crisis must have eligible preconditions, a causal chain, and a recorded outcome. AI policies must respect authority, information, budget, and implementation capacity. Unobserved regions must remain uncertain. Global systems must not update every entity at tactical frequency.

##### Safety and presentation gates
No operational real-world mass-harm instructions. No glorification of civilian suffering. No collective blame. No fabricated casualty reports, family testimony, or historical records. No rewards for escalation, atrocities, civilian harm, or human extinction. Preserve the explicit navigation-aid and instrument-approach exclusion of ILS, VOR, TACAN, NDB, DME, RNAV procedures, and instrument approaches unless the user explicitly changes it.

Delivery of this document is a specification milestone. It is an implementation milestone only when the repository has been audited, the selected vertical slices are integrated, regression tests pass, performance is measured, saves migrate safely, and the known limitations are documented. A written requirement is never proof that code exists.

##### Unified regression and release gates

Before release:
- Verify that injury, death, missing, capture, and medical withdrawal are distinct states.
- Verify that every status transition has a valid source and timestamp.
- Verify that no injury record creates duplicate people or duplicate casualties.
- Verify that no medically withdrawn person is assigned to an incompatible combat role.
- Verify that reassignment does not erase prior service or qualifications.
- Verify that a disability does not automatically block all employment or leadership.
- Verify that healthcare and assistive-device availability are finite but do not create arbitrary instant cures or instant permanent outcomes.
- Verify that private medical information is protected in UI, exports, news, multiplayer, and logs.
- Verify save migration from existing and earlier supported versions.
- Run all existing flight, avionics, sensor, campaign, economy, population, multiplayer, and performance regression suites.
